subtopic: STATUTE LAW (CANADIAN CHARTER OF RIGHTS AND FREEDOMS) AMENDMENT ACT MEASURE TO AMEND

speechtext: The House resumed from Friday, March 29, consideration of the motion of Mr. Crosbie that Bill C-27, an Act to amend certain Acts having regard to the Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms, be read the second time and referred to the Standing Committee on Justice and Legal Affairs.

subtopic: STATUTE LAW (CANADIAN CHARTER OF RIGHTS AND FREEDOMS) AMENDMENT ACT MEASURE TO AMEND
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I confess to have been looking forward to debating the Government's proposal to implement the equality provisions of the Charter of Rights coming into effect, as they do, in the middle of this month.
In the previous Government we were at work on preparing to face up to the fact that many of our laws contain measures which create inequalities in our society. A project had begun where a group of law officers of the Crown had been given the task of reviewing statutes, over 1,000 in number, in light of the equality provisions of the Charter. They were to make recommendations to the Government for the removal of any aspect of discrimination, unfairness or inequality in those statutes. We did this because Parliament should act to remove these inequalities in order to bring our laws into compliance with the Charter to save ordinary citizens, particularly those who were disadvantaged under the present law, from the hardship, difficulty and costs of taking their cases to court. There is, of course, no doubt that they can take their cases to court because the Charter is now the law of Canada and the equality provisions will become part of that law as of April 18. In my submission and that of my Party it is not appropriate for Parliament to be engaged now in a decision about what the Charter should be. That is already settled, it is the law. How it is to be interpreted is a question for the courts to decide in the final analysis.
What we ought to have been doing is looking at all of the legislation in the country, following up on the project which had been begun, and changing that legislation to bring it up to the high standard which the Charter of Rights and Freedoms has established. Well, the present Government recognized its
responsibility. If I can quote the Minister of Justice (Mr. Crosbie) in his discussion paper Equality Issues in Federal Law, and I intend to return to this again during the course of my remarks, the Minister noted at page 6:
Section 15 reinforces the responsibility that governments have to shape laws, policies and programs to the goal of equality-
I would have judged this legislation by the Minister's own standard, that is, the responsibility of governments to shape laws to the goal of equality. Let us look at Bill C-27 and discover how close the Government has come to achieving the goal of equality by way of its legislation.
I think I can sum it up with a statement made by the Minister himself in a speech in Quebec City. He was talking about the responsibilities of removing discrimination and bringing our laws up to the high standard required by the Charter. He ended on a wistful note quoting from Robert Browning, saying: "Ah, but a man's reach should exceed his grasp, Or what's a heaven for?" By that he meant that there will inevitably be a shortfall between what we would like to do with regard to removing discrimination and what we will actually achieve. According to Robert Browning and the Minister, that is sort of a good thing because it leaves room for progress and movement.
However, it is tragic that there is such a tremendous shortfall between what will be attainable and what the Government is required to do by the Charter. There is such a shortfall that Bill C-27 can only be called a cop-out and a very inadequate effort, if it can be called an effort at all to live up to the responsibilities imposed on government by the Charter.
The national Government should have assumed leadership in encouraging the provinces, which also have legislative responsibilities, to bring their own laws into compliance with the Charter. Far from providing leadership to the provinces, the Government seems to have reinforced a do-nothing approach. It has left it to the underprivileged groups in society which do not have equality under the law to go to court and argue their case.
I would like to remind Canadians that the national Government did not welcome the three-year period of time which was given to it and other governments to bring laws into compliance with the Charter. We would have preferred a shorter period of time, or no time at all, so that when the Charter was implemented in 1982 the process of bringing the laws into compliance with the Charter would have been overdue. We were pressured by the provinces to give them a period of time. Eventually three years was agreed to.

April 1, 1985
Statute Law Amendment Act
I would have hoped that the federal Government would have done its duty in that three-year period and would also have encouraged the provinces to do theirs. On the contrary, we now have legislation which does very little and which leaves private interest groups to continue to argue their cases. After I have gone through the legislation I want to turn to the other half of this package, the work of the parliamentary committee, and give my views and the views of my Party on its work.
What is in the Bill that has been put before us? Most of it is contained in Part V, the reform. This so-called reform is a very poor substitute for a true effort to bring the laws of Canada into compliance with the Charter equality provisions. Most of the changes are artificial, semantic, and without very much consequence. The greatest number of amendments are devoted to Acts governing merchant seaman, laker pilots and returned soldiers. Last week in the House one of the members of the Conservative Party argued that the very thickness of the Bill was some evidence of an effort by the Government to do something.
However, when you think of the small group of individuals in society that is affected by the merchant seamen legislation, the laker pilot legislation and the returned soldier legislation, you can see how very little has been done in the Bill. This is a group of Canadians who are entitled to have the laws that affect them brought into compliance with the Charter. However, when one looks at the amendments that are made in their interest, one can see how very little there is. Clause 74 and Clause 97 amend the Army Benevolent Fund Act and the Returned Soldiers' Insurance Act, adding widowers to those who can receive payments from the Fund. While that is fair, of course, it is very little.
Clauses 75 through 83 amend the Bankruptcy Act and present us with what can only be called non-amendments. Monumental and courageous changes are not to be found here. The Government has merely substituted the word "spouse" for the phrase "husband and wife" and the word "child" for the phrase "son and daughter". Clause 83, which amends subsection 190(2) of the Act, makes a recognition that debtors may be female as well as male and thus substitutes the phrase "debtors' creditors" for "his creditors". These are hardly what could be called the reform that the country was expecting when the Charter equality provisions were to come into effect.
Clauses 84 through 89 lower the minimum age for potential directors of co-op associations and applicants for farm syndicate loans from 21 years old to 18 years old. While this is a form of progress, these are changes which are nothing more than a recognition of the change of the age of majority which has been in effect in our country for the last 15 years. Such an amendment shows that the Government is lagging far behind the new realities brought forward in the implementation of the Charter. It would not be so bad to have these changes if some serious reform was also included in the legislation. However, it is obvious that nothing else has been added.
Clauses 90 to 93 amend the Merchant Seamen Compensation Act but they are also rather inconsequential. They substitute the phrase "surviving spouse" for the expression "widow or invalid widower". One must wonder if this is the limit of the imagination of the Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) and his Government in reforming the legislation. Where are the new ideas and new approaches that were promised by the Prime Minister?
Clauses 94 and 95 amend the Pilotage Act. Certain provisions have been deleted as a factor in the calculation of the interval between medical examinations. Now, pilots who are 55 years of age and over are required to submit to an examination only once every three years instead of once a year. We must note that no change is made in the rule which demands mandatory retirement of pilots at age 65.
Next, clauses 98 through 103, which amend the Canada Shipping Act, allow for the possibility that a woman who owns a ship will transfer it by marriage to her husband and that men may be mortgagees of the vessel transferred to them. Also, they substitute the words "mental disability" for "lunacy" and include "husband" in the definition of a near relative. In other words, it is a set of semantic changes that recognize that women, in relation to the Canada Shipping Act, may be carrying on the activities that are carried on by men.
We know that the rules of statutory interpretation recognize all of this anyway. Under the rules of statutory interpretation, "his" can be taken to mean "hers" where appropriate, such as in a case like this.
This is really a semantic exercise to which we have been treated by the Government. It is not at all an exercise in bringing the laws into compliance with the Charter requirement that there be no discrimination but fairness and equality.
Clause 104, which amends the Veterans Rehabilitation Act, eliminates the distinction between 16-year old boys and 17-year old girls, as far as the language of the statute is concerned. Again, it is not significant.
That is the sum and substance of the legislation. Taken as a whole, all of these changes show no attempt to instil our legislation with the same spirit that ensured the inclusion of Section 15 of the Charter. They mark a dismal failure on the part of the Government to perform its legislative duty. What is presented to the Canadian people is a mere recognition of language, semantic equality, and nothing of the social realities and possibilities. There is not to be found here any transformation of legislation which is commensurate with the high value placed by Canadians on the idea of equality.
The Government had an answer when it was criticized for doing pathetically little in the legislation: the Government not only prepared legislation but prepared a discussion paper. The Government established a subcommittee of the Justice Committee and I am pleased to be a member of that subcommittee. I can say that my Party intends to co-operate and support the work of that subcommittee. The Hon. Member for Mount Royal (Mrs. Finestone) will be spending a lot of time working
April 1, 1985

on that committee and will be the lead spokesman for our Party. We continue to believe that the concept of setting up that committee, giving it such a short time limit and a wide mandate and keeping it in the dark about some very important questions, shows that the Government is not serious about wanting to achieve equality.
I want to elaborate for a moment on some of the problems we see with the committee. In the first place we wanted a Charter of Rights and Freedoms for all Canadians because we recognized that even with the fundamental decency that characterizes Canadian society, there are minority groups and groups with a minority perspective that do not have the total and absolute approval of Canadian public opinion. The battle of these groups to achieve equality will be a tough one. They will be battling against public opinion. There is an educational job, in a sense, to be done to inform the Canadian people about the meaning to these minority groups of the kind of discrimination and hardship which is part of their daily lives. I refer, for example, to the handicapped for whom a great deal needs to be done to bring them to a positon of fair equality and access with other Canadians, to the benefit of our Canadian society. We recognized that by entrenching rights in the Charter for minority groups, by providing that these are rights recognized by law, they cannot be taken away from these groups by Parliament or by the legislatures. One recalls the ringing statements of our former Prime Minister, the Right Hon. Pierre Elliot Trudeau. We were telling the Canadian people that their legislators can go so far but no further in diminishing their rights. That is what the Charter is about.
What is the discussion paper about? What is the committee about? It is another round robin exercise where the very groups we want to protect from majority public opinion will be submitted to the pressure of majority public opinion in the analysis of their rights.
I talked about the handicapped a moment ago. Let me pursue that. One of the things we anticipate is that providing equality for handicapped groups in our society will cost and may cost some pretty big bucks. It may be, for example, that every public building in this country will have to have a ramp entrance provided so that the handicapped in wheelchairs will be able to enter. There are no entrances like that in the Parliament Buildings right now. If they are to be provided and if the law will require that, I can see a government as cost-conscious and as fanatically dedicated to deficit reduction as this Government wanting to deny that kind of construction program across the country or wanting to phase it in over an unfairly long period of time.
In light of this kind of consideration, the chance of handicapped groups doing well and getting their rights before the kind of committee and in the kind of process which will be set up is not very likely. I say the same in connection with retirees who are retiring because they are required to by law. Are those laws valid? A committee is being asked to look at the question. There will be a kind of controversy before the committee. I
Statute Law Amendment Act
suppose some groups will think about promotions which will not be available if mandatory retirement is removed. Some groups will be arguing that mandatory retirement should continue because of a vested interest. Others will see a vested interest on the other side. The decision will not be made on the basis of Charter principles. I am afraid a parliamentary committee will act the way a parliamentary committee should act. It will try to figure out what is public opinion. While I say that is the way it should act, in a sense it is regrettable that democracy works that way. It was because of a recognition that democracy works that way that we entrenched fundamental rights which are now for the courts to determine, not for legislatures, this Parliament or this parliamentary committee to determine.
I had a great deal more which I wanted to say, but in my remaining minute I want to indicate the wrong-headedness of dealing with this problem in the way the Government has. I call upon the Government to let us know what legal opinions it has received on the requirements to change legislation to comply with the Charter. That is really the way in which a parliamentary committee, if it is to operate, should operate. We are being kept in the dark about a process which I should like to describe in this thumbnail sketch. I think the law officers of the Crown did their job. They looked at over a thousand laws. They made legal opinions in many cases. Some of them might be deemed controversial, but in many cases they were able to give the Government advice that "this provision needs to be changed, that provision needs to be changed and probably this one does".
Did the Government bring forward the changes which were recommended? I do not think it did. I think it brought forward the absolute bare minimum and ignored the advice of the officers of the Crown. It will be one of our main purposes as a committee to try to find out from the Government what the law officers of the Crown have been saying and what are the many laws which ought to be changed. Let us go about doing our business, not just changing the grammar or gender in ways that really do not make any difference to anyone, given the Interpretation Act. Let us bring in the real changes which will make our laws comply with the equality provisions of the Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms.

subtopic: STATUTE LAW (CANADIAN CHARTER OF RIGHTS AND FREEDOMS) AMENDMENT ACT MEASURE TO AMEND
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am pleased to speak on Bill C-27 because it has at least one provision which, if allowed to stand, will cause a very grave injustice. Generally, as previous speakers have said, this Bill does not do very much. The arrangement of three years ago was that three years after the Charter came into force the Government, having had time to review the laws, would bring them into line with all provisions of the Charter, particularly the equality ones. As has been said by our critic, the Hon. Member for Burnaby (Mr. Robinson), and by other speakers, very little was done on substantive questions such as the equality of women. There were just a few little word changes.
However, one change has been made which some people might have overlooked. It could endanger the lives of refugees or of their families back home. Clause 112 makes a change

April 1, 1985
Statute Law Amendment Act
which is against the interests and even the personal safety of refugees and their families.
First I refer to the old Subsections 29(2) and (3) of the Immigration Act. This is when a person has come to the airport and said "I am a refugee from another country". He then goes to an inquiry. In that inquiry he is supposed to make his claim to be a refugee. Subsection (2) states:
At the request or with the permission of the person with respect to whom an inquiry is to be held, an adjudicator shall allow any person to attend an inquiry if such attendance is not likely to impede the inquiry.
That is to say, at the request of the person who may be going to declare his refugee claim. If he or she wants other people to attend, they may be allowed to attend. Subsection (3) is very clear:
Except as provided in subsection (2), an inquiry by an adjudicator shall be held in camera.
There was good reason for that law. It was to protect the person who, as a result of his or her situation at that point, had to be one of the weakest and most defenceless people within our borders. That is being changed in this proposed law. It now reads:
An inquiry by an adjudicator may, on application therefor, be held in camera if it is established to the satisfaction of the adjudicator that the person with respect to whom the inquiry is to be held, or any interest of Her Majesty, as the case may be, would be adversely affected if the inquiry were conducted in public.
In other words, it is no longer given to the refugee claimant to say whether he wants the inquiry held in camera, whether he wants other people attending. How he or she may make that request and be overruled by the adjudicator.
I am not aware of any reason being given for this change. This is not one of the important changes, such as those previous speakers mentioned in the Shipping Act and so on. This change could cost the person his or her life or the life of a member of the family. It is very strange that, in the interest of justice, the Charter and equality, the Government should have chosen to make such a perverse and dangerous change in what was otherwise a satisfactory law.
The Government has a strange notion of equality. We see that illustrated in other sections of the Act; for example, with regard to women. With regard to the rights of a person applying for unemployment insurance while pregnant, we have the Bliss decision which says there is no discrimination against women on account of a decision against a person for being pregnant. You would think that the Supreme Court in that case was of the opinion that men or women could equally become pregnant. At any rate, there should have been an attempt to correct that in this law to make it clear that women should be protected fully, even when they are pregnant; but that was not done.
Likewise with the disabled, a committee had many hearings about the disabled and the disabled made many recommendations, some of them key recommendations; yet there is practically nothing reflecting that in this Act. The only thing that
affects it is the change of one word in the Shipping Act concerning lunacy. Nothing else was done for the disabled.
In those cases it appears there is a perverse concept of equality and equal justice. The concept allows for the strong to be aggressive towards the weak. It says the Government should not interfere, in a contest between the strong and the weak, on behalf of the weak. Whether a person is weak personally and individually, perhaps physically, or whether a person is weak through belonging to a group which is at a disadvantage in society, the principle of justice would be that the law would give special protection to the weak.
Our law does that very clearly in another matter, a matter that is not reflected in this law today. I want to give it as an example. Nobody in his right mind would challenge it. Our Criminal Code makes it an offence for an adult to seek sexual relations with a child in a manner which, if the adult sought sexual relations with another adult, would not violate the Criminal Code. In other words, there is a concept of free choice which it is considered can be made by an adult, but cannot clearly be made by a child because the child could be under pressure or, being a child, ignorant. Therefore, an adult is not entitled to take advantage of a child because in that sense the child is considered weaker than the adult. That concept is in our law. It is a sound principle, a principle of justice. It does not say that the strong, in that case the adult, has equal rights with the weak, in that case the child.
We have made some progress in the Criminal Code with regard to assault by men against women, even married men against their wives. It has been clarified. On the whole whatever is the wording, the clear indication was that what was being done was to protect the person who might be physically weaker than the other and who also might be at an economic disadvantage because of her membership in an economically disadvantaged group.
That is the correct way to go to protect the weak against the strong. If there is a conflict of rights, as there very often is, then the obligation of a just, honourable and humane society is to ensure that, above all, the rights of the weak are protected. This is a principle that has been put forward very eloquently in the last couple of years by the bishops of the Roman Catholic Church in Canada. They talked about the preferential option for the poor. They do not say that we have to give the rich and poor equal rights in all matters, or equal consideration, equal help or equal support. They say that the poor need special support, special protection because they are poor, because they do not have the strength of money and power.
In this case we are dealing with people who are extremely weak, extremely powerless. A man or woman may come here on the run from another country, perhaps with children, in fear of their lives. They come to Canada and they want to be refugees. If this law is adopted in the form asked for by the Government, they will have to make that declaration in an open court if the adjudicator decides that they do not have good reason for holding the inquiry in camera. The benefit of the doubt is with the adjudicator instead, as before, being with the refugee claimant.
April 1, 1985

What good purpose is served by this change? I cannot imagine that it benefits the adjudicator to have that power of choice absolutely in his or her hands and which originally was absolutely in the hands of the refugee claimant. I cannot see how the adjudicator loses by letting the refugee claimant make the decision whether others should be allowed in the hearing or not.
Perhaps a media reporter may want to come in. The media reporter might lose in the sense that on that day he or she may not be able to write a story about a human interest case. There might be some genuine loss or deprivation to a reporter in that sense, but consider the other side. If news of that person's refugee claim comes out in a public way and that person is known to have made certain accusations against the Government of his or her country, and if that person's refugee claim is not sustained in Canada, and many times that happens, that person must return to his or her country to a government that has learned that he or she made as unfavourable statement. That person might be persecuted or have his or her life endangered. I know Canada has a commitment not to refuse people who would be in danger if they were to return to their own country even when they are not accepted here. However, how does a refugee claimant know that he will be accorded that kind of protection? How does he know that that judgment will be made in his favour and that he will not be sent home? Further, how does he know that his wife, brother or sister back home may not be persecuted on account of the news that he made a refugee declaration in Canada? There is simply no comparison between the possibility of a media reporter being deprived of an interesting story and the possibility of a refugee or a refugee's relative being persecuted and perhaps killed because of a story that was published.
I have not heard anyone who deals with refugees, any of the lawyers, church people, ethnic, immigrant or community groups, make any complaint about the old Subsection 29(2) and (3) of this law. None of them has suggested that it is unjust. I have not heard any complaint from immigration officials indicating that that Section is unjust. I have not heard of any reason why that Section should be changed. I very much urge the Government, in committee, to reconsider Clause 112 of this law and delete it. Otherwise, the Government may have the blood of innocent refugee claimants or their families on its hands.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it is with suitable humility that I address the House today on behalf of the people of Ottawa-Carleton. I am pleased to address a Bill of my choosing in this Chamber for the first time.
As you know, Mr. Speaker, my riding is not far from here. Some Hon. Members live in Ottawa-Carleton. For those who
Statute Law Amendment Act
do not, I can assure them that it represents a cross-section of Canada and has a challenging mixture of urban and rural areas. It has a linguistic balance of our two official languages that is a remarkable reflection of our country.
Bill C-27, an Act to amend certain Acts having regard to the Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms, was first introduced to the House on January 31, 1985, along with a discussion paper entitled Equality Issues in Federal Law written by the Hon. Minister of Justice and Attorney General (Mr. Crosbie), a man for whom my respect, esteem and personal indebtedness is second to none.

The Minister also announced the appointment of a special subcommittee of the House, before which Canadians across Canada will be able to express their views. This committee can and should serve as a privileged access to parliamentarians for minority groups who want to explain the kind of changes they would like to see in our legislation.

Bill C-27 proposes to bring 50 federal statutes into conformity with our Charter of Rights and Freedoms that will come into effect on April 17, 1985. That date is an important one in Canadian history. On April 17, 1855, Charlottetown became a city. As we all know, the British North America Act evolved in Charlottetown a few years later.
In 1982 federal lawyers began a systematic review of the statutes to see where amendments were needed to ensure compliance. This was an enormous undertaking as there are more than 1,100 federal laws of general application. As did the Minister, I too offer them my congratulations for the success of their tedious task.

This Bill will amend the Bankruptcy Act, the Food and Drugs Act, the Weights and Measures Act, the Customs Act, the National Parks Act, the Returned Soldiers' Insurance Act and other legislation.

In short, it will have an impact on the lives of the people of my riding as well as all Canadians. It will have an impact on the lives of my immediate family, some of whom are in the Chamber today. My pride in representing them is one that has taught me the importance of family, friends, loyalty and the determination to do what is right when it is right, at the right time. For this I am grateful.

The riding of Ottawa-Carleton has both rich and poor neighbourhoods, a number of small businesses, and a very substantial federal presence-the National Research Council, to be exact.

In recent times it has been represented by the Right Hon. Member for Vancouver Quadra (Mr. Turner), Mrs. Jean Pigott and the Hon. Jean-Luc Pepin. In fact, on February 17,

April 1, 1985
Statute Law Amendment Act
1977, in what she called her bachelor speech, Mrs. Pigott also addressed issues concerning Canadian human rights when she spoke so eloquently of the discrimination against handicapped Canadians. We have come some distance since then but there is much further to go. The Terry Foxes and Steve Fonyos of our country have made us acutely aware of the fact that our handicapped are also our people.
When you land at the Ottawa International Airport, Mr. Speaker, you are in my riding. As you taxi along the tarmac, I ask you to think of previous Tory candidates who paved the way for my political success, candidates like Colonel Strome Galloway, Bill Neville, Jean Pigott and Bert Lawrence.
In the area of equality rights, the review of federal statutes by Bill C-27 turned up some inconsistencies including, for example, inconsistencies in the age of majority. Some statutes require a person to be 18 years of age whereas others require the age of 21. It underlined some outworn assumptions, particularly the assumption that breadwinners are always men and dependants always women. It identified some social conventions that may or may not stand up to court challenges under Section 15 of the Charter; in particular, mandatory retirement at the age of 65.
The Hon. Member for Glengarry-Prescott-Russell (Mr. Boudria), my eastern political neighbour, referred to mandatory retirement at age 65 as being discriminatory, and I agree with him. However, Senator Croll's study of a few years ago indicated that a very small percentage of Canadians wish to continue working at age 65. They should, however, be given that option. Our population is aging and we will need their presence, their experience, their skills and knowledge and their will to go on working in a meaningful way.

There is no easy answer. We must find out what Canadians want. First we will listen, then we shall act.

When I think of human rights and equality in Canada, I am reminded of the tremendous violent discriminations that are occurring in many countries of the world like the Republic of South Africa, Sri Lanka, the Soviet Union and many Latin American countries. I am also reminded of the peace, order and good government that is the general rule of law here at home. I will concede that we have our problems, such as discrimination in the Indian Act, but Bill C-31 is finally attempting to eliminate some of this discrimination. As a member of the Standing Committee on Indian Affairs and Northern Development, I can testify to the intense effort that we are all making in that regard.
We can only have equality when we are all equal, and even our great democracy has some kilometres to run. Although I shall be out of the country on April 17, I will take time to pause for a few moments as Canada takes a large step in the maturing process of nationhood. I will also renew my pledge to this nation.

Although I am not a lawyer, I realize that action must be taken to improve the compliance of our laws with the Charter, and it must be done before April 17. Bill C-27 is an important step in the right direction.

It is also in accordance with one of the themes of social justice underlined in the Speech from the Throne of November 5, 1984, as read by Her Excellency the Governor General. She said:
My Government is determined to ensure that social justice in Canada keeps pace with the changing needs and circumstances of our people.
The new Government continues to pursue and support economic equality for women because we can only have equality when we are all equal in all respects. Let us replace the
expression vive la difference with vive I'egalite.
The new Government is increasing employment opportunities for women in government and its agencies. It is also preparing amendments to the Divorce Act. The new Government will seek provincial co-operation in providing additional assistance to the victims of family violence, including child abuse which is a most despicable and regrettably increasing human act.
On a recent visit to Quebec City, Mr. Speaker, during a tour of the new musee du Seminaire, I was warmly reminded of the fundamental importance of the family in a painting of the holy family with Jesus helping Mary and Joseph at the carpentry bench. Increased family violence is a clear signal that the most important foundation of our entire civilization is being threatened.

Mr. Speaker, the Hon. Member for York South-Weston (Mr. Nunziata) said that his Party would vote in favour of Bill C-27. He also added-

We will continue to press for full equality. We want to ensure that equality becomes a reality in the very near future.
So does this Government and so do I. The Hon. Member for Burnaby (Mr. Robinson), who has also spoken during this debate, said that the disabled and handicapped-
-should demand that the Government finally accept its responsibility to change laws to implement full equality for the disabled.
I agree, Mr. Speaker, so let us not take forever to do this. The Hon. Member for Broadview-Greenwood (Ms. McDonald) indicated that Bill C-27 has been referred to as housekeeping legislation. Perhaps it is, but usually when one cleans a house very thoroughly, one has to first rearrange some furniture. Bill C-27 is doing just that. The special committee chaired by my colleague, the Hon. Member for Etobicoke-Lakeshore (Mr. Boyer), has been given a significant responsibility, as was described by the Hon. Member for Gloucester (Mr. Clinch) in this debate. He said, and I quote:
April 1, 1985

The Government considers it most important that we have the widest possible consultations with the people of Canada.
Sometimes our actions are better judged by the way outsiders see us, and I would like to read from an editorial entitled "A Better Canadian Way" which was reprinted from the Washington Post in the international Herald-Tribune on November 17, 1984, and I quote:
Mr. Mulroney is going to try another method, a series of consultations throughout his country to work toward a common purpose.
[ Translation]
Mr. Speaker, we shall soon be ratifying Bill C-27, but I sincerely hope that the special committee that will shortly be sitting in a number of Canadian cities will also reach its conclusions as soon as possible. We must get to work in order to give the word "equality" more meaning and adopt the amendments that Canadian women, the disabled, minority groups and others have been demanding so desperately. [English]
We are maturing as a nation, Mr. Speaker. We are growing as a people and we are able to stand up as an example to the whole world as a nation of honesty, integrity, compassion and fairness. The only limitations we have in this country are the ones we place upon ourselves. Let us speak more of our pride, of our successes and of our accomplishments, and let us learn from our shortcomings and our failures. Bill C-27 is paving part of a path to April 17 when every individual will become equal before and under the law. I am proud to have added in this small way to part of that pathway.
Let me conclude, Mr. Speaker, by telling you a true story. Fifteen years ago I was living and working in a village in northern Tanzania in East Africa. It was called Kiswani. As we drove by the village one day, we stopped at a water fountain to get something to drink. A young girl was standing there and she saw me get out of the Land Rover with my binoculars around my neck. She was somewhat fascinated by these binoculars as she had never seen any before. I bent down and let her look through them. All of a sudden the faraway village and houses became very close to her. She was fascinated by this. That young black girl clasped my hand and took me down a dusty road to her village. She was saying mzungu wangu which means "my white man". She had adopted me on the spot. I was indelibly impressed by that moment because that lovely innocent little child had no fear, no discrimination and no prejudices. That, to me, Mr. Speaker, is what life should be all about.

Hon. Warren Allmand (Notre-Dame-de-Grace-Lachine
East): Mr. Speaker, April 17 will be a very important day in the history of Canada because on that day Section 15 of the Charter will come into effect. Because people follow this debate at different times, I think I should refer for a minute to Section 15. It will guarantee for Canadians equality before the law despite their race, religion, ethnic origin, sex, age and so on. It will assure that they will not be discriminated against on those bases. What is very important about Section 15 is that it is a constitutional provision, which means that it cannot be amended unless the federal Parliament and seven provinces representing 50 per cent of the population agree to do it together. So that Section is very secure against hasty amendment.
Secondly, it is extremely important because, as it is in the Constitution, it prevails over every other federal and provincial law. This means that any ordinary law passed by a federal or provincial Parliament will be subject to the anti-discrimination provisions of Section 15. That section will strike down many of the discriminatory laws and regulations and practices we have had in this country for many years.
Many of those here now and who were here in the last Parliament will know that I voted against the Charter and the constitutional Bill on the final vote. I did so for very specific reasons, but not because I was against Section 15, an entrenched Charter of Rights or an amending formula. As a matter of fact, I was fully supportive of the constitutional package when it came out of the joint committee near the end of June, 1981. However, once the provinces got hold of that constitutional package in the early fall, they almost took apart many of its outstanding provisions and left it in a very weakened condition. In particular, it was the provinces which imposed the inclusion of the famous "notwithstanding" clause in Section 33. This meant, in effect, that a province or the federal Parliament can pass a law overriding Section 2 of the Charter, dealing with fundamental freedoms, as well as overriding Section 7 to Section 15, including Section 15, by simply saying in their ordinary statute: "Notwithstanding Section 7 or Section 8 or Section 15 of the Charter, we legislate as follows and our law will prevail". That sort of opting out of those provisions of the Charter is permitted for five years and can be repeated again.
That, Mr. Speaker, was one of the things which led me to vote against the final package. Despite the fact that I was in favour of many things in the Charter, I could not tolerate that and I thought some Members should rise and vote against it on that basis. I of course was also very disappointed with the amendment the provinces imposed with respect to aboriginal rights and language rights. As a matter of fact, in the Charter right now there is inequality in the sections respecting language rights.
The Hon. Minister of Employment and Immigration (Miss MacDonald) is here and I might say, because she intervened in this debate, that I think the House should know that most of the provinces who fought against an entrenched Charter of Rights were Conservative Governments; not the Government of Ontario or the Government of New Brunswick, but the western provinces and Nova Scotia and Newfoundland did oppose those sections. They were successful in knocking out the section dealing with women in the early fall of 1981, and successful in knocking out the aboriginal rights section. It was only after large demonstrations on Parliament Hill that compromise sections were put back in the Charter. We must remember that there were many, not her but many Members of her Party, who fought against entrenchment for many years. They were against it in principle. There were some Conservative Governments and Conservative Members in this House who favoured an entrenched Charter of Rights, but a lot of them did not and a lot of Conservative provincial premiers did not.
While Section 15 was passed into law in 1982, its implementation, was delayed for three years so that the provinces, the federal Government, private groups and associations and businesses could prepare for its implementation because it could and will have very far-ranging effects. That three years was to be used for preparation of such things as the provision of ramps and access for disabled people, and so on, which
April 1, 1985

requires time and money. It always had been the view of the previous Government to bring in a Bill which would bring all federal laws and ordinances into line with the equality provisions of the Charter.
I was a member of the Standing Committee on Justice and Legal Affairs over the last four or five years and every time the Minister appeared on Estimates I asked him about the review which was underway to bring federal laws and regulations into accord with the Charter, especially with Section 15. He would report progress to me on every occasion. We were moving ahead. Of course, the reason for that, as has been mentioned, was that despite the fact that Section 15 would go into effect on April 17, 1985, we did not want to leave it to ordinary citizens and their small resources to go to court to prove that certain laws were ultra vires with respect to Section 15. We thought it would be better, and everybody agreed, to bring in a Bill which would bring into line our federal laws and thereby save individuals, businesses and groups from spending a lot of money on going to court to prove their point in accordance with the equality provisions of the Charter.
The present Government has brought in a similar type of Bill, the Bill we are discussing today, to amend 50 laws which require changes in accordance with the Charter. However, only 11 of those 50 relate to changes with respect to the equality section. The changes that Bill C-27 will implement are, for the most part, very minor. It changes the word "husband" to the word "spouse" and uses the word "persons". The Bill is very limited, timid and minimal. It does not attempt to bring into line many of the controversial laws of Canada which will probably be challenged in court unless something is done quickly.
Our position is that although the Bill moves in the right direction, making necessary amendments to federal laws, it does not go far enough. It does not cover many of the areas it should have. Rather than addressing those issues in the Bill, the Government has published Equality Issues in Federal Law: A Discussion Paper. This discussion paper lists most of the controversial issues. A Justice subcommittee has been asked to hear evidence across the country with respect to these issues and to produce a report.
I will mention some of the issues contained in this discussion paper, but which are not in the Bill, which that committee will deal with. They include discrimination on the basis of age, mandatory retirement provisions, and provisions for age of minority. Those issues are not dealt with in the Bill. They were left for the subcommittee to discuss across the country. Also left out of the Bill are issues relating to sexual discrimination. Those issues are subjected to discussion across the country. Also left out are issues with respect to disabled people.
It may be reasonable to have discussions across the country if we had not had them in recent years. However, several years ago the Royal Commission on the Status of Women dealt with many areas of discrimination against women. The evidence and report are still available to be examined. We had a report
Statute Law Amendment Act
entitled Obstacles which dealt with discrimination against disabled people. Parliamentarians in the last Parliament spent more than a year travelling across the country and listening to evidence with respect to discrimination against disabled people. A special task force of Parliament dealt with racial discrimination and discrimination against visible minorities. It produced an excellent report called Equality Now. The Special Committee on Indian Self-Government dealt with many issues of discrimination against Canadian Indians. There was a special committee in the Senate which dealt with the problems of the aged and aging just a few years ago.
These issues have been studied, discussed and consulted on. It is time to move ahead. The problem is that many of those issues require tough decisions. It seems that the Government does not want to make decisions. It is going to travel across the country and consult on these issues one more time and then make recommendations.
I wonder how credible the consultative process of the subcommittee will be. I am not casting aspersions on the Chairman who is sitting the House today. However, as the subcommittee travels across the country it will hear many of the same things that were heard by the Obstacles committee and the Equality Now committee. Will they take it seriously? Will the decisions be made by the members of the subcommittee on the basis of that evidence, or will the decisions be made by the Cabinet and caucus here in Ottawa, regardless of what is said to that committee in different parts of the country?
I hope that after listening to the evidence across the country the committee will recommend the tough choices to be made. So far I have been given no hope in that respect because we have not seen to many Conservative back-benchers coming forward with recommendations or conclusions which are at variance with the Government. We will wait and see what happens as a result of that committee.
I would like to put our position again very succinctly, Mr. Speaker. The Bill should have covered a much wider area in order to save Canadians from going to court to prove that they have equality rights such as will be implemented by Section 15 on April 17. The Bill should have covered a much wider area to save litigation fees and loss of time. In the last few years the court challenges program applied only to constitutional challenges with respect to language rights and minority education. Many of us hope that that program will be expanded to help people who have no means of raising funds to go to court to prove their case with respect to the equality provisions. That is very important.
What is the use of implementing charters of rights with entrenched rights and of having human rights and language rights legislation if the people who would benefit cannot go to court because they do not have the resources to make these challenges? If it is to be meaningful for the minorities in the country, something must be done to help them challenge laws, practices and regulations to allow them their rights and justice in accordance with Section 15.
I am pleased to note that the women of the country are organizing themselves very well. They are organizing a fund to

April 1, 1985
Statute Law Amendment Act
permit them to go to court when necessary to assure their rights in accordance with the Constitution. Many groups are able to do that because they are big enough and have the necessary connections. However, others do not, and I hope the Government will expand the court challenges program to enable people to take advantage of their rights in the Charter.
I urge the members of the Justice committee to consider expansion of Bill C-27 into areas it has not already addressed so that immediately after the passage of the Bill Canadians will understand where they stand with respect to their entrenched rights.

Mr. Speaker, I am not clear as to the purport of the Hon. Member's question, but if he is asking why Section 15 of the Charter was not drafted in such a way as to avoid any misinterpretations of federal laws and statutes, then my answer is that the Constitution deals with general provisions. It does not deal with detailed provisions.
All constitutions are the same. The American and French Constitutions do not go into detail with respect to every situation in life. They pronounce on certain great principles. Section 15 pronounces on anti-discrimination situations and situations of equality before the law. It would have been completely unreasonable to refer to all the statutes that would be affected under Section 15 of the Charter. Section 15 of the Charter will apply to all federal laws, all situations and all practices.
That is the way it is in the United States. There are general provisions in the human rights amendments to the constitution. It was over many years that groups in the United States were able to prove that their rights were being violated by certain state and federal laws and that the constitution prevailed with respect to equality. Many laws in the United States discriminated with respect to the equality of black people. I believe it was only in 1954 that the famous Brown case was ruled on by the Supreme Court of the United States in accordance with the general principles in the American Bill of Rights. The court said that those laws in the South which
segregated blacks and whites in education and socially were illegal.
My answer is that the Constitution cannot and should not get into the details of every federal law, statute, regulation and so on. The Constitution provides for principles in general terms and that is what we have done. As soon as this section was drafted and passed by the House, by Parliament and all but one of the provinces, the Government immediately took a review of all federal laws to see which ones might be in contravention of the principle enunciated in Section 15. It was the Government's intention to put forward a Bill which would remove those discriminatory sections. As a result of the leadership conventions and the election, the Bill was never passed.
While I am pleased that the Government is following this up, the Bill it has introduced is too limited in its scope. It is on that basis that I object to it.

Mr. Speaker, the Party that I represent, the New Democratic Party, and its predecessor, the CCF, had from the beginning of its foundation back in the 1930s supported the idea that there should be inserted into Canada's Constitution a bill of rights. Although the Hon. Member for Notre-Dame-de-Grace-Lachine East (Mr. Allmand) indicated a moment or two ago the NDP Premier of Saskatchewan during the debate disagreed with that policy, it was a fundamental principle our Party had adopted and supported over these many years. Because we believed in it, we supported the inclusion during the constitutional debate in the Constitution of Canada of a Charter of Rights. We did so because we remembered so many instances in Canadian history when the rights of individuals or groups had been very seriously restricted.
Let me mention a few of those. We had the situation in the Province of Quebec when the then Union Nationale Government headed by Premier Duplessis persecuted and prosecuted the Jehovah's Witnesses. We had a situation in western Canada in my province of Manitoba, in Saskatchewan and in Alberta when numerous groups, including municipal leaders, had called for restrictions on the rights of the Hutterite communities to live as they wished and to expand their colonies as their populations grew.
We had a situation during World War II in which we are now all agreed that a tremendous injustice was done to the Japanese people then living in the Province of British Columbia. When Canada went to war with Japan, all people of Japanese origin, both citizens and non-citizens, none of whom had been involved in espionage or sabotage, were moved from their homes to other parts of Canada. They lost their

April 1, 1985
Statute Law Amendment Act
homes and businesses. They experienced tremendous difficulties. This move was made only because they were Japanese.
In the Province of Newfoundland when the International Woodworkers of America Union tried to organize the people who worked in the forests of Newfoundland, very repressive legislation was brought forward by then Premier Smallwood and that union was destroyed.
Because we knew Canada's record had not always been what it should be, we supported the proposal that the Charter of Rights be included in our Constitution. We did so particularly because we realized that in recent years there has been a tremendous movement into Canada of large numbers of immigrants from countries where the language spoken is neither English nor French. For example, from Italy, Spain, Portugal, from eastern European countries including Yugoslavia, Hungary and Poland, and even more so from countries in Asia and Africa with their non-white populations. We realize this movement has created and would create among many people living in Canada feelings of prejudice and discrimination. We all know about the feelings of prejudice and discrimination against the original habitants of Canada. I am referring to our native people, most of whom live in poverty. They have the poorest education, the poorest housing, the lowest health standards and the highest rate of unemployment of any Canadians. Because of those kinds of situations, we supported the passage of the Charter of Rights. We had hoped when it came to reviewing the legislation, which ought to be changed because their provisions are not in conformity with the principles included in the Charter, that the Government would recognize that many of our laws, regulations and policies conflict in important ways with the principles set out in the Charter of Rights and Freedoms, not just in Section 15, Mr. Speaker, but in many other sections.
We Find the Government and the Official Opposition have not dealt with these important questions that should have been dealt with. I refer to a few of them, such as freedom of association, freedom of speech and fundamental legal rights which our citizens should have. These are just a few issues that have to be dealt with but which are ignored in this Bill.
This Bill avoids dealing with the most important human rights issues which confront us. Essentially what we have is a housekeeping Bill. As my colleague the Hon. Member for Burnaby (Mr. Robinson) has indicated, we will support it realizing that it is a very small step in the direction in which we must move.
Let me deal with some of the issues and problems not dealt with in this Bill and which I believe should have been dealt with. Unless they are dealt with and unless some of the laws are changed, what we will see in the next few years is a large number of important human rights cases that will wend their way from the lower courts up to the Supreme Court of Canada before they are decided. This will create difficulties for people who feel they are not being fairly treated, not being dealt with as the provisions of the Charter say they should be People will therefore have to take their cases to court, which will take years and tremendous expense will be involved.
Let me deal with a few of the issues which I believe should have been dealt with. First is the principle of freedom of speech. Most Canadians believe they have the right to say what they want to say, but there are important restrictions on what they can say. I should like to give a few illustrations of that fact.
It is still an offence to subject the courts to public contempt or ridicule. In 1969 a university student in the Maritimes went to jail for 10 days for writing and publishing an article indicating that a certain trial was a mockery of justice and that the courts were instruments of the corporate elite in the decisions which they made. The courts say that people who speak about them have to avoid invective. If someone writing about the courts avoids invective, readers will not even want to read it.
Defamatory libel is still in the Criminal Code. To injure a person's reputation by subjecting him or her to public hatred, contempt or ridicule, is an offence. In 1969 the Georgia Strait newspaper in Vancouver was prosecuted and convicted because it gave its Pontius Pilate award for justice to a judge and that was judged a criminal offence in Canada. I am not defending that newspaper, but when the courts can come down hard on such a newspaper, we know that our freedom of speech is restricted.
I remember a case which occurred in the first few years that I was a Member of Parliament, in about 1963. It involved a resident of Montreal who wrote a letter to the editor of La Presse, Gerard Pelletier. In that letter the resident was extremely critical of a sentence which a judge in Montreal had imposed on someone who was charged and convicted. I am not concerned about whether or not the decision of the judge was right or wrong, but if a person disagreeing with a sentence imposed can be prosecuted-and I think the person in this case spent a little time in jail and Mr. Pelletier had to apologize for the judge for printing the letter-it indicates that there are some pretty important restraints on the ability of people in Canada to say what they want and not fear being penalized.
I should like to point to the Official Secrets Act, which needs to be revised in a major way. In its provisions there are very wide prohibitions on the unauthorized disclosure of government information. We know how many documents produced by government have been marked secret or confidential. Also we know that on occasions when public servants felt that governments were doing things that were wrong, they leaked the documents and information either to members of the Opposition or to people in the media. That was very prevalent in the last year or two before the 1984 general election. The provisions of the Official Secrets Act cry out for major revision.
Let me look at the War Measures Act which has been used on a number of occasions in a Draconian way, to say the least. Many sections of that Act go beyond any suggestion of demonstrable justification. The Act needs to be drastically revised. The present Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Turner),
April 1, 1985

when he was Minister of Justice, promised that there would be such a revision. Despite all the promises made by him, the former Prime Minister, Mr. Trudeau, and others in government, that was never done.
I do not want to refight the battles we fought at the time the War Measures Act was used by the former Government, nor do I want to debate at this time whether what it did was necessary. However, I remind Hon. Members that more than 350 people in the Province of Quebec were picked up, incarcerated and held without the opportunity to see their lawyers. After some time they were all released. Not a single one of them was charged or convicted of any offense. We all now agree that the War Measures Act should have been amended long before now. I call upon the Government to look at it and to bring in amendments to that Act in the very near future. The alternative to that would be, as I indicated earlier, court cases which may take years and cost a great deal of money, not to say a great deal of effort.
I want to deal with some other problems which are not dealt with and cannot be dealt with even if the Charter included every provision it should. I urge Hon. Members to look at the report of the Special Committee on Visible Minorities in Canadian Society entitled Equality Now! It was issued just about a year ago and looked into the problems of our visible minorities, namely the non-white minority citizens of Canada. It found that their situation was very difficult. It found that there was a great deal of prejudice and discrimination in employment, housing and education against the very large number of non-white Canadians, including many newer immigrants and, of course, the native population. That committee recommended that all roadblocks preventing full participation of these people in the cultural, social, economic and political life of the country be eliminated. We know we have a long way to go if we are to achieve that goal.
I ask Hon. Members to think about a very simple question and try to answer it. How many members of our visible minorities in any city in Canada represented by any Member of Parliament can be found in occupations such as police officer or firefighter? In the City of Winnipeg, which has a large native population, there is not a single native police officer or firefighter. There is a large population of non-white people and native people in my city. We have over 25,000 people of Philippine descent, as well as large East Indian, Sikh and black populations, but one would have to use a high-powered microscope to find any of them in the fields which I have mentioned. Sometimes their exclusion has been obtained by deliberate intent, sometimes through unintentional restrictions which restrict their rights; for example, height or weight regulations or requirements for formal education which they do not have. For these new immigrants, the Charter alone will not make them fit easily into our country as full partners. That report called for language training programs to be expanded. It called for funding for ethnic racial groups, for ethnic organizations, for broadly-based community organizations which provide a service to help make the transition and to integrate these newer Canadians.
Statute Law Amendment Act
In the field of employment we have to adopt an aggressive affirmative action program. I commend the Minister on the statement she made last week that the Government intends to proceed in this way. subtopic: CALL FOR ESTABLISHMENT OF PARLIAMENTARY COMMITTEE
CALL FOR ESTABLISHMENT OF PARLIAMENTARY COMMITTEE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, since September 4 a vibrant and meaningful multicultural policy has been painfully absent. As such, the profile and political clout of multiculturalism have suffered considerably. In the end, of course, it is the minority communities that are the real losers. In an attempt to safeguard and foster a more respectable and rightful place for multiculturalism, I urge the Government to establish a permanent and separate Standing Committee on Multiculturalism.
Presently the multicultural Minister reports to the Standing Committee on Communications and Culture. The unfortunate and predictable result under this Tory Government, has been that the multicultural Minister has taken a third seat behind the Minister of Communications (Mr. Masse) and the Secretary of State (Mr. McLean), who also report to the same standing committee. As a consequence, multiculturalism is a poor and dead last in this three-way shuffle.
A distinct standing committee would go a long way in protecting the multicultural policies which former Liberal Governments had fought so hard to attain. It would also enable the many significant issues to be properly addressed and examined. In keeping with the coming into effect on April 17 of Section 15 of the Charter of Rights and Freedoms, the timing of establishing a standing committee on multiculturalism could not be better. I only hope, as do our ethnocultural communities, that the Government does not kill this proposal through study and procrastination.
April 1, 1985

subtopic: REFORM URGED ON BASIS OF ELECTED CHAMBER
REFORM URGED ON BASIS OF ELECTED CHAMBER
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the Fathers of Confederation were wise men. In devising the form of government for the Canada they envisioned, they made sure the population of each province would be represented by Members of Parliament in the House of Commons, and then, to prevent the MPs from the heavier populated provinces penalizing the lower populated provinces with legislation that would hurt those regions, they created a Senate. But after more than a century the Upper House is no longer protecting the regions and minorities, and Canadians throughout the nation are calling for reform or abolition.
Thousands of Canadians not only want an elected Senate, but also desire equal representation from all provinces. In a Triple E setup, Members of the House of Commons would represent the population of each province. The Senators would protect the regions and minorities. With that setup any Government would think twice about legislation that would hurt a region or the people. Canada is a great country. We have a Government oriented to the will of the people. With a Triple E Senate we can realize our great potential.
I believe such a reformed Senate, elected, equal, and efficient, in our far flung nation could mean the salvation of the Canada we have known.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I should like to give notice today of the intention of the Government to introduce a Bill to resolve an issue with which I am sure all Hon. Members are familiar. The Government intends to table on Wednesday a Bill to make supplementary equalization payments to the six provinces which currently receive equalization payments. Members will ask why legislation is required to authorize these supplementary equalization payments. The Government must introduce new legislation because there is no legal requirement or obligation on the part of the Government of Canada to make these payments.
The obligation remains, however, to administer the system of equalization based upon the fundamental principle of fairness. This principle must govern our actions even while our own fiscal situation is difficult. It is this Government's recognition of the fundamental principle of fairness which signifies our unswerving desire to work with our partners in the provinces and to assist them wherever possible, for that is the essence of our Confederation.
April 1, 1985

Under existing legislation, equalization payments to some provinces will actually decline in 1985-86 as a result of the expiry of the three-year transitional payments that were provided for in 1982. I have carefully considered representations from these and other provinces which receive equalization payments. In addition, I have been governed by the prevailing necessity to control a crippling federal deficit which in paying the interest charges alone costs the people of Canada $1 out of every $3 they pay in federal taxes.
What we propose in the Bill under these circumstances is a fair and equitable solution to the issue of supplementary equalization. The amounts are substantial although some may have desired more. However the principle of fairness underlying our Confederation has been maintained.
I should like to indicate briefly some of the considerations that guided our decision in this matter. The primary consideration was the impact from the expiry of the three-year transitional provisions. When the new equalization formula was introduced in 1982, it was anticipated that some provinces might suffer a decline in their equalization entitlements, and it was expected that the transitional provisions would allow time for provinces to adapt to the new formula. There are also provisions in the current formula for floor payments to prevent severe year to year declines in equalization payments. Newfoundland, New Brunswick and Prince Edward Island were guaranteed a 95 per cent floor, and Nova Scotia, Quebec and Manitoba were guaranteed lesser amounts, given the relatively greater fiscal strength of these three provinces.
In determining the amounts of the supplementary equalization payments to be provided in this Bill, it was decided to calculate the payments to Quebec, Manitoba and Nova Scotia as the additional equalization amounts they would receive if a 95 per cent floor applied to them over the next two fiscal years. It was further decided that Newfoundland, New Brunswick and Prince Edward Island should receive the same per capita supplementary payments as the average for the other three recipient provinces.

This measure will consist in providing supplementary equalization payments for 1985-86 of $110 million for Quebec, $50 million for Manitoba, $20 million each for Nova Scotia and New Bruswick, $15 million for Newfoundland and $5 million for Prince Edward Island.
In addition, since present projections indicate that Manitoba will experience a further decline in its equalization payments in 1986-87, the Bill will contain provision to make a further payment of $65 million to Manitoba in that year.
The total supplementary payments in 1985-86 will amount to $220 million. This is in addition to the regular equalization payments of over $5 billion. This means that the total regular and supplementary equalization payments to provinces in 1985-86 will amount to almost $5.3 billion.
Supplementary Equalization Payments
These amounts are substantial and should help these provinces to meet their responsibilities in providing essential services. They will mean an increase in the deficit projected for the coming year, and given the Government's serious financial situation they are the most we can provide.
I should note that these payments are totally unconditional and are made in addition to the other substantial transfers to the provinces, particularly in respect of insured health services and post-secondary education under the established programs financing arrangements. The total fiscal transfers from the federal Government to provincial Governments for equalization and the established programs financing arrangements will amount to some $20.7 billion in 1985-86-some $1 billion higher than the $19.7 billion being transferred during the current fiscal year.
I reiterate that legislation to authorize these supplementary equalization payments is necessary because there is no legal obligation or requirement on the federal Government to make these payments under existing fiscal arrangements legislation. The necessity is one of fairness for all Canadians.
[ Translation]
The supplementary equalization payments measure taken by the Federal Government is an extremely generous one, considering the Government's present financial situation. It acknowledges the present financial situation of the provinces in question and reflects this Government's intention and desire to work together with the provinces and to assist them when possible.

In concluding, Mr. Speaker, may I point out that the present equalization program expires on March 31, 1987. We recognize that the system is not perfect and we will be consulting with the provinces to establish a new formula for the period of 1987 to 1992. Such actions will be a major part of the general review of the federal-provincial fiscal arrangements which will be undertaken over the next two years by both levels of government. I look forward to meeting with provincial Finance Ministers later this year to begin discussions of the fiscal arrangements that will apply during the 1987 to 1992 period.
We shall continue working together towards the common goal of making Canada a better and fairer place for Canadians from all regions, all provinces, all walks of life.
[ Translation]

speechtext:

I believe it is the first time in the history of Canada that we have had a Budget by instalments like the one we are now having, which began in November. They tested the water and went with the program. Rather than carrying on with making the same amount of equalization payments, the Government tried to cut more than the provinces could take. They come today to reinstate some of the money. However, there are still some major shortfalls. What is happening today re-establishes a little bit of the money that was taken away some months ago. When the mini-budget was proposed in November, the situation was very bleak.
[ Translation]
For instance, the Province of Quebec is being given $110 million today. However, the Quebec Government was asking for $163 million and is only getting $110 million more. In fact, under the formula we extended for one year last year, the Quebec Government should have received $273 million, but it is only going to get $110 million.
This is no big deal. They are being given $163 million. I am not saying that I am upset. The Government is restoring some of the funds it cut rather unrealistically last fall, but if we look at the cuts that affected Quebec last November, we see that $770 million worth of federal activities will not take place in Quebec because of the cutbacks. So if we add $163 million, this means nearly $1 billion Quebec has not been getting since the Progressive Conservatives have been in power.

The same situation applies in the Maritimes. The Maritimes gained back $80 million, but there is still a shortfall of $74 million. The cuts of November were $400 million as they affect the situation in the Maritimes. I could go on. They are reinstating some money for Manitoba, but not all the money to which that province is entitled if the federal Government were to fulfil its constitutional obligation.
As I said earlier, this is a budget by instalment. We now have something on equalization payments because the Minister is preparing the ground. Last week he lost some money to the oil industry. He is now preparing the ground for a big tax increase. We are waiting for that day. Some announcement will be made to try and consolidate their political position. The reality will come in May, if it is not postponed again.
It will be almost a year since this Party came to power and it has not yet been able to put all the pieces together. It made promises to everybody. It cut back some. It is a real show. The real strip-tease will be the Budget presented by the Minister of Finance (Mr. Wilson). Today is a great day. They had to admit to the NDP House Leader that it is not true that they will not increase taxes. Get ready, guys, it is going to come to us soon, in the neck! They waited in order to try and consolidate their political base. The reality is they got elected by making all sorts of irresponsible promises. Today they are reinstating some but not all of the money.
The provinces do not have what the Constitution calls for, but it is an increase, a step in the right direction. I do not blame the Minister for that. I am just sorry that they are not giving the money to which the provinces are entitled under the Constitution. This is the problem. This test has not been met. I understand. I have a lot of sympathy for the Minister of Finance. He lost his battle with the Minister of National Health and Welfare (Mr. Epp), he lost his battle with the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources (Miss Carney), and he lost his battle with the Minister of Employment and Immigration (Miss MacDonald). A decent Minister of Finance would have resigned with so many lost battles, but we will give this Minister another chance. He is now preparing the ground for the budget. It is going to be his last day in the House of Commons when Canadians, especially the taxpayers, get it in the neck come the end of May. In the meantime, we keep smiling.

Later in this House, in answer to questions by myself, he tried to state that the federal Government's financial position was worse vis-a-vis that of the recipient provinces. I believe that is a position which is completely indefensible.
Throughout the period of this Conservative Government, it has pretended that it was some kind of surprise to find that there was an actual decline in the money that would be going to the provinces as a result of the 1982 legislation. Yet in 1982 Conservative Opposition Members stood with Members of the New Democratic Party like the Hon. Member for Winnipeg-Birds Hill (Mr. Blaikie) and fought against the equalization formula the Liberal Government had then introduced. Some of those Members are now members of the Cabinet and they must act upon the words they spoke in 1982. I for one am glad that the Government has made a partial reinstatement of the money to those provinces.
Although this announcement will benefit a number of provinces, it is obvious to all that it was the New Democratic Party Government of Manitoba that led and forced the fight on this issue. The Manitoba Government, along with a coalition of representatives from labour, health, education and social services groups, confronted the federal Government. To a degree, they were successful. It is their victory and we in the House
April 1, 1985

should give them that credit. When the legislation comes before the House, we will deal with it further.
At this time I would like to say that there are still concerns with which we must deal. We need more information about what the provinces will actually receive in 1986-87. That should be the underlying principle that the Government will take with it into the next round of negotiations.

In taking into account this principle of fairness, we decided that we should establish some rationale for dealing with the shortfall. That was, as I indicated in my remarks, to establish a 95 per cent floor for the three provinces which suffered the shortfall.
