speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Liberal Party
subtopic: STATUTE LAW (CANADIAN CHARTER OF RIGHTS AND FREEDOMS) AMENDMENT ACT MEASURE TO AMEND
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, before lunch I had started to make a few comments on the Bill before the House today, namely, Bill C-27, an Act to amend certain Acts having regard to the Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms. I would like to start by reminding the House that when the Constitution Act, 1982, was proclaimed on April 17, 1982, the provisions of the Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms became effective. However, the provisions relating to equality rights as set forth in Section 15 of the Charter were not to come into effect until April 17 of this year. Section 32(2) reads as follows, and I quote:
April 1, 1985

Notwithstanding subsection (1), section 15 shall not have effect until three years after this section comes into force.
Therefore, April 15 of this year will mark the anniversary of the proclamation of the Charter and the date on which Section 15 becomes effective.
Mr. Speaker, the House will recall that the Liberal Government at the time had undertaken to examine and review all federal statutes to check their compliance with all provisions of the Charter.
Section 15 is a major provision of the Charter which must be interpreted within its general context. Section 15 acknowledges the right of every individual not to be exposed to any discrimination on the basis of race, national or ethnic origin, colour, religion, sex, age or mental or physical disability. The wording of Section 15 reads as follows, and I quote:
Every individual is equal before and under the law and has the right to the equal protection and equal benefit of the law without discrimination and, in particular, without discrimination based on race, national or ethnic origin, colour, religion, sex, age or mental or physical disability.
Subsection (1) does not preclude any law, program or activity that has as its object the amelioration of conditions of disadvantaged individuals or groups including those that are disadvantaged because of race, national or ethnic origin, colour, religion, sex, age or mental or physical disability.
Mr. Speaker, these rights are subject only to such reasonable limits prescribed by law as can be demonstrably justified in a free and democratic society. That is Section 1 of the Charter of Rights and Freedoms.
We can also refer to Section 27 which deals with multicul-turalism and its importance to this country, and to Section 28 by which rights are guaranteed equally to both sexes. Although hundreds of cases have been brought before the courts on the basis of various provisions of the Charter, Section 15, since it has yet to become effective, has not been the subject of any judicial interpretation. After the three-year waiting period ending on April 17, Canadians could expect the Federal Government would table a Bill providing appropriate amendments to laws that are not consistent with the Charter and especially with Section 15, so that the amendments could be adopted in time for the coming into effect of Section 15 on April 17 of this year, thus sparing Canadians the need to undertake costly court proceedings to have their rights recognized.
Mr. Speaker, these amendments are necessary to eliminate the discrepancies that exist in our federal and provincial statutes, to help Canadians avoid situations that may be humiliating and unfair in addition to being extremely costly, and to improve the clarity and fairness of Canadian laws.
Mr. Speaker, the burden of proof often lies with minority groups. These groups often have to prove they should be considered first-class citizens. All these groups, including the disabled, visible minorities and language minorities have, at some time, been exposed to the discrimination and racism that surface, from time to time and to our shame, in our society.
Statute Law Amendment Act
Mr. Speaker, I must remind the House that the language issue, for example, is in fact covered under Sections 133 and 93 of the BN A Act of 1867, not to mention Manitoba Act Section 23 which deals with the same rights as those included in Section 133 of the BN A Act of 1867, namely access to legislatures and courts. In addition, we have Section 23 of the Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms concerning linguistic rights. To this day, those four sections could be challenged before the courts for legal interpretation. We had the court challenges program funded by the Secretary of State which, along with legal advice from the Minister of Justice, enabled Canadians to test Canadian legislation or test the system to make sure that the various Acts were correctly interpreted.
Mr. Speaker, Hon. Members will recall that less than ten days ago I asked the Secretary of State (Mr. McLean) and the Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) what would replace the court challenges program on April 1 since, as we all know, this program ended March 31, yesterday. There is no money left, therefore no program, and that is unfortunate! Since 1978, Mr. Speaker, when the then Liberal Government had established the court challenges program, 14 cases have been accepted, which represents an over-all amount of $580,000, and during the fiscal year ended yesterday, we had $260,000 to help Canadians uphold their rights before the courts by contesting, if you will, the interpretation of Sections 133 and 93 of 1867, and Section 23 of the Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms. That is no longer available.
As you may recall, Mr. Speaker, I had asked the Secretary of State whether he was seriously considering the feasibility of expanding the court challenges program to include Charter Section 15. I, for one, am firmly convinced that it is essential to help those minority groups who may be among the most underprivileged, who do not always have enough money, and who must necessarily rely on federal Government financial assistance. I had asked the Minister if he thought the program might be expanded.
In his answer the Minister said:
-as the Hon. Member rightly notes, with the widened context of Section 15, there are a number of groups that are very anxious to pursue rights and to see that these are clarified. In the review that is on-going, the wider context is also being reviewed in terms of support that may be offered.
That is found at page 3292 of Hansard, March 22, 1985.
[ Translation]
Mr. Speaker, the Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms is important to us and, personally, I would not be against this Government helping minority groups and people who feel their rights are being infringed on in connection with the section on official languages and the provision dealing with equality, namely Charter Section 15.

April 1, 1985
Statute Law Amendment Act
Bill C-27 now under consideration amends fifty Acts. With respect to legal rights, there are Sections 7 to 9 and 11 of the Charter, fundamental freedoms under Section 2, mobility rights under Section 6, and minor amendments to Section 15, amendments which amount to revised wording rather than genuine implementation of the Charter or a clear indication of what it means. Mr. Speaker, instead of making comprehensive amendments to the most controversial measures concerning minority groups, the Government once again opts for further study, and a committee will go traipsing across the country to seek the views of Canadians, again forcing minority groups to defend anew the rights they had finally acquired in 1982.
This extra work, this requirement to appear before a committee means more briefs, more studies and lengthy proceedings during which a committee may listen with sympathy, but where the majority or any given lobby group can turn the whole exercise into what ends up being a very humiliating experience for many people. Minorities resent coming under public scrutiny over and over again to prove that they are right and to reconfirm whether the rights they thought they had acquired in 1982 are indeed equality rights, Canadian rights they do have and which should command full respect.
Mr. Speaker, here are some remarks made recently by the Hon. Member for York Centre (Mr. Kaplan):
The purpose of the Charter of Rights was indeed to protect minorities against pressure from the majority. By disregarding such considerations and shirking its responsibilities to give full force to the Charter, the Conservative Government violates the very spirit of that instrument.
In my opinion, Mr. Speaker, that is a pretty fair analysis of the situation. Minority groups will now have to appear before that parliamentary committee which, for many of us, had held hearings in 1981-82 here in Ottawa and elsewhere in the province. We were hoping and thinking that, by adopting the Charter of Rights and Freedoms, all Canadian legislation would have been reviewed after three years to eliminate discrepancies related to Section 15. Such is not the case. As I said earlier, the Bill introduced last January by the Conservative Government amends fifty Acts. It seems that the provinces are doing the same thing, and we are still waiting to see who will put and end to all this by finally settling this major issue.
Part V of the Bill concerning equality rights-there are 30 provisions out of a total of 120-amends eleven federal Acts. In most cases, these amendments do nothing more that than substitute the word "spouse" for the words "husband or wife", the word "child" for the words "son" or "daughter", the words "surviving spouse" for "widow" or "widower". Semantics, Mr. Speaker! The other categories of amendments relate to age, and one amendment to the Canada Shipping Act substitutes the expression "mental disability" for the word "lunacy". Mr. Speaker, none of those changes is controversial, of course. We have been doing that for years in an attempt to standardize our legislation and avoid anomalies.
Mr. Speaker, I said earlier that the provincial legislatures were strongly opposed to the inclusion of the equality rights provision throughout the constitutional debate, finally relenting in November 1981, except for the Province of Quebec, of course. Well, those legislatures have not been in any particular hurry to amend Acts of theirs that might conflict with the Charter of Rights.
The Progressive Conservative Government in Ottawa now has the same attitude and, as far as I can see, is not providing any leadership at all, which might have the effect of strengthening the position of the provinces. Believe it or not, they have only reached the following stage: Ontario, for instance, has published a 400-page compilation of sections to be amended, while Alberta, Newfoundland and Saskatchewan have published a white paper containing proposed amendments. Mr. Speaker, we have been waiting for three years!
Quebec has systematically invoked the notwithstanding clause in Section 133-a clause I find abhorrent-thereby removing all legislation from the field of application of Sections 2, 7 and 15 of the Charter and giving only its own Charter force of law. New Brunswick has passed a law eliminating major problems of non-conformity for which, it deserves to be congratulated. British Columbia, Manitoba, Nova Scotia and Prince Edward Island have taken no public initiative, but we have been informed that working documents for the white paper are being drafted. Mr. Speaker, they all know that Section 15 will be proclaimed on April 17, 1985.
They are dragging their feet. They are waiting and examining and consulting! The Federal Government has started a consultation process through a parliamentary committee that will try to understand what Canadians think of all the grey areas referred to in the working document, the Minister's white paper: Equality Issues in Federal Law-distinctions made on the basis of age, mandatory retirement and economic and social problems. All these issues are of great concern to many Canadians but should have been dealt with by now, and a Bill tabled in this House that could stand the test and be used to consider in the House the intrinsic value of these issues. But no, they are going to let a committee find out what Canadians think about mandatory retirement, although Section 15 clearly prohibits discrimination on the basis of age. I think it is all quite clear and straightforward, Mr. Speaker. Why not let the courts decide? We have gone through the parliamentary process. We have done what was necessary. Let the courts and the legal experts tell us what the legislator had in mind. So much was clear to many of us. Why drag it all again in front of the general public to attract attention and possibly arouse public reaction? We see what is happening in New Brunswick with a document published by the Government. It is not easy to be a minority. It is not easy to be disabled. It is not easy to be one of those groups that are always being examined to death to find out whether they do or do not have this or that right, because the Charter is quite straightforward and quite clear.
Mr. Speaker, I see you are warning me that my time has expired or is about to expire. I would have a lot more to say about this subject. I am sorry the Government was unable to
April 1, 1985

table a general and comprehensive Bill that could be used as a working document to establish once and for all for Canadians that there is only one Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms and one law for everyone.

Mr. Speaker, I thank the Hon. Member for York Centre for his question. The issue is a major one because, as I said in my remarks, minority groups more often than not are destitute, without much money. Maybe the Government wants to terminate the legal assistance program. Last week, I asked the same question from the Secretary of State, I asked him as I said in my remarks, whether he could extend the program to cover Section 15. He answered he had that under consideration. For my part, Mr. Speaker, I feel that if our society is to be just and fair, it is imperative that the majority, that is the taxpayers should help by means of an administered program, if you wish, in an impartial way, in order that individuals and groups may submit their cases to the courts which are in my view the resource, the forum open to us when the validity of a statute is challenged. I think for instance that the Canadian Bar could be consulted by this Government. If the Government wants to stay away from the day-to-day administration of the program to avoid conflicts, I would be very reluctant to have the program extended and entrusted to the Minister of Justice. I do not think he can simultaneously act as solicitor and judge, as client and counsel, but I would be in favour of that Government having a legal assitance program that would cover not only Sections 133, 93 and 23 of the Constitution, but also Section 15, and having a board of directors set up with membership from the civil liberties union, for instance, or the Fondation des droits de l'homme, including one or two representatives from the Canadian Bar. The Government could also have a representative on that board which would be provided with government funding and would have
Statute Law Amendment Act
the responsibility and perhaps the duty to financially support legal cases of groups and individuals wanting to challenge certain constitutional sections-and I repeat certain constitutional sections-because not everyone is in a position to finance such important cases, like the Forest Case, for instance, in Manitoba, which has established that Section 133 and Section 23 were the same thing. That cost close to $75,000. The efforts and the money did not come from Mr. Forest personally, but this has established something. If someone is challenging for instance the right for the Government to enforce retirement at 65, and is suggesting that this is unconstitutional, I think that each and every Canadian is entitled to know exactly what the views of the courts are on that, and to know exactly and definitely that the courts are in agreement or disagreement with the Constitution and how the latter should be interpreted. To me, it is absolutely vital that we have an extended program, a program administered if you wish independently from the Government, but a well-funded and well-organized program.

speechtext: The House resumed consideration of the motion of Mr. Crosbie that Bill C-27, an Act to amend certain Acts having regard to the Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms, be read the second time and referred to the Standing Committee on Justice and Legal Affairs.

April 1, 1985
Statute Law Amendment Act

subtopic: STATUTE LAW (CANADIAN CHARTER OF RIGHTS AND FREEDOMS) AMENDMENT ACT MEASURE TO AMEND
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, this debate on Bill C-27 is just one more step, perhaps a small step, in the long and enduring quest for equality. There can be no more important cause than that in a democratic society. That is why I am particularly honoured by Members of this House to have been chosen as Chairman of the Subcommittee on Equality Rights. Our committee will now be looking at the number of issues raised under federal statutes in light of Section 15 of the Charter. Because of that I have been present in the House for many speeches that have been given on Bill C-27.
I would like at this time to make some general observations and comments to put a number of the issues raised in context. I should preface this by saying that it has been my political credo and I believe very strongly in fair shares for all and special privileges for none. With that in mind, I think the current subject before us is one that gives an opportunity to make that principle an even greater reality. None of us should be so pretentious as to assert that any single Bill before the House or any single measure at one point in time or, indeed, anything such as Section 15 of the Charter is the be-all and end-all.
What we are engaged in is an enduring struggle to see that the ideals of our democracy, the equality of its citizens before and under the law, can be in fact a reality. As we know, under Section 15 of the Charter discrimination is prohibited, such as discrimination on the basis of sex and religion.
I would like to turn briefly to the pages of Canadian history to show how long this quest for equality has been. Dealing for a moment with the question of sexual discrimination, the right of women to be candidates for election at both the federal and provincial levels generally came with or followed the extension of the franchise to women. If we just look at the dates on which women were given the legal right to be candidates in Canada, we find a very important story there.
Manitoba was the first province giving women the right to be candidates for election to the Manitoba legislature on January 28, 1916; Saskatchewan followed on March 14, 1916; Alberta on April 19, 1916; British Columbia, the following year, in 1917; Nova Scotia in 1918; then Ontario in 1919. In that same year this Parliament passed a law entitling women to be candidates for election to Parliament. It was not until 1922 that Prince Edward Island came on board, and in 1925 Newfoundland, before its entry into Confederation, of course. New Brunswick passed such legislation in 1934, and Quebec on April 24, 1940. There is a 24-year period during which legislation was enacted to establish the legal right of women to be candidates seeking public office in the legislatures of this country and in Parliament. It says something about the nature of the country that it took virtually a quarter of a century for that right to be developed equally from coast to coast so that all women could share that right.
Another of the anti-discriminatory provisions now in the Charter deals with religion. I think here it is important to understand something of the background. I will do so by citing an example from my book entitled Political Rights which
looks back into the history of the qualifications required for people to be elected to our assemblies.
Since Confederation no religious qualification has been required of Members, nor have clergymen of any denomination been disqualified. Under the Constitution Act of 1791 clergymen were disqualified from becoming Members of the Assemblies of Upper and Lower Canada. In New Brunswick, even after the turn of this century, clergymen of all denominations were disqualified for election. Such provisions did not reflect an anti-clerical tradition so much as they manifested the principle of separation of church and state. That point alone is worth emphasizing because in the work that lies ahead of our Subcommittee on Equality Rights, we must not only look at the face of the law as we find it on the statute books but go beyond and behind it to try to understand the economic, the social, or the cultural policy on which those laws were enacted. It will be very important to ensure there is no unravelling of important social relationships or distortion of long-standing values that are important to the public of this country. I think the separation of church and state is a principle to which many held and still hold in some instances.
Certainly different was the case in Nova Scotia where an anti-Catholic legal requirement was emblazoned in the statute books of that province. Up to 1830 Members of both Houses of Nova Scotia's Legislature were required, before taking their seats, to make and to subscribe to declarations against tran-substantiation, the invocation of saints and the sacrifice of mass, as practised in the Church of Rome. This requirement was expressly remitted by the King in the case of a Member from Cape Breton who had been elected in 1820, and a decade later in 1830, such declarations renouncing the Roman Catholic religion were wholly abolished by an act of the legislature.
Those are but two of the many examples from the fabric of Canadian history that show that the struggle we now have to deal with discrimination and eradicate it from our statutes is something of a quest on which Canadians have been engaged from the time this nation first began.
Clearly the pace has been accelerating, Mr. Speaker. I would like to place the current Bill C-27 in a somewhat more recent historical context. If we look at the year 1947 and the post-war emphasis on reconstructing a new order out of the devastation left by World War II and on the importance of reasserting the roots of democratic societies, we find in the Province of Ontario in that year the introduction of a racial discrimination Act. Very shortly after that, other provinces followed suit. By 1951, provinces began legislating fair accommodation and fair employment practices Acts. In 1960 here in Parliament, the Canadian Bill of Rights was enacted. Fifteen years later, it could be said that by 1975, all provinces of this country had established Human Rights Commissions. The year after that, in 1976, Canada ratified two major United Nations' human rights covenants. It was in the following year, in 1977, that the Canadian Human Rights Act established a federal Human Rights Commission and consolidated other existing federal human rights legislation.
April 1, 1985

By 1980 a movement had begun here to establish a Charter of Rights and Freedoms. This was included in the federal proposed resolution to amend the Canadian Constitution. The ins and outs of that battle are well known to all Members of the House. It was really two years there after, on April 17, 1982, that Her Majesty proclaimed the new Constitution Act, 1982 and that Section 15 of that Act would come into effect three years hence, which will be on April 17, just a few days away.
There has been much activity which can and should in the near term lead to further changes. We have had the report of the Special Committee on Visible Minorities in Canadian Society entitled Equality Now! It was tabled in the House in March, 1984. Also we received the Abella Commission report on equality in employment, as well as a discussion paper of the Minister of Justice (Mr. Crosbie) on equality issues in federal law. It is clear in considering Bill C-27 that it is but one measure in an area which is exceedingly active in Canadian legislatures and in the minds and movements of those who care about developing a truly democratic society. We have never had a greater amount of activity than is the case today. Not only do we have Bill C-27 before us and the prospect of our parliamentary committee doing its work and reporting back to Parliament in the near future, but we have a criminal law review under way which is raising many Charter-based issues. As all Hon. Members of the House know, the Indian Act is now under revision aimed particularly at resolving a number of the sexual equality issues found there. Legislation is being challenged before the Supreme Court of Canada with respect to the provisions of the Lord's Day Act in light of Charter provisions. The Unemployment Insurance Act is under review, also in relation to Charter provisions, as well as many other economic and relevant considerations. The list continues. I have marked at least seven major areas apart from the work now before the House in which the present Government is currently engaged, areas dealing with the quest for equality and fairness in Canadian public policy, Canadian law and the practices of the federal Government.
I have heard in the House statements by opposition Members to the effect that Bill C-27 is only a small step or a half-way measure. Rhetorically they have stated that it is too little in light of what must be done. I would certainly agree with those comments if Bill C-27 were all that we had before us. I hope what I have just said leaves the picture as clear as it can be. This is but one part of a great effort which is now being made by a new Government strengthened with a clear mandate from the people to make changes and to get on with implementing recommendations, policies and ideas which have been around for quite a while. That is most certainly what motivates me. If Hon. Members opposite can be supportive of this endeavour, let them join with us and avoid trying to score rather narrow partisan points on a matter as profoundly important as this one, because then we could really make great strides for the country.
Statute Law Amendment Act
Bill C-27 should not be diminished. As someone who has worked closely with over 140 statutes during the last five years in writing my books on election law, I readily appreciate the hours and hours which have gone into combing through federal statutes to pull out the discrepancies, distinctions and discriminatory provisions which exist on the face of the more than 1,100 statutes. This Bill therefore represents no small effort in and of itself. It justifiably represents an important first step. However, more important, it is fundamental to our approach that the solutions to the problems of equality in Canadian law not be dictated from Ottawa but, rather, be arrived at through speaking with and listening to the people of the country. If anything was said last September 4, I think it was a very clear statement that the era in which Ottawa knows best and Ottawa tells Canada that this and that is what the laws will be is an era which is over.
We will come forward with a program based upon a consultative process. We will try to relate the complexities of modern government to the realities we face and the continuing ideals of Canadians living in a democratic society.

Mr. Speaker, the in-depth review of Federal statutes to ensure that they reflect the equal status of all Canadians in accordance with Section 15 of the Charter has resulted, first, in the introduction of Bill C-27, and second, in the creation of the Committee on Equal Rights.
Bill C-27 proposes amendments to a number of Federal acts related to legal matters. Under its terms of reference the committee will examine the Federal statutes related to economic, social and cultural matters on which present legislation is based. The Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms must be interpreted on the basis of our social standards. We, as Members of the committee, must therefore allow every Canadian to express his views. We are now developing a participatory process, and our recommendations will have to reflect daily facts of life as well as the provisions of Section 15. In other words, Bill C-27 and the work of our committee will be the starting point in the recognition process of human rights. For these reasons, Mr. Speaker, we are favourably impressed with the mandate of our committee.

We have a task to find laws which will curb the powerful and will uphold the weak, laws which will give meaning to the principle stated in Section 15 of the Charter that all Canadians are equal before the law and equal under the law. Those who would lament the fact that today we do not have the last word or the definitive answer on all policies raised in the federal statutes, particularly those of the Liberal Party who have been critical of this, must in fairness recognize that the review in the Department of Justice was not begun on this subject until a mere seven months before that Party was driven from office. In short, there was a singular lack of dispatch in getting down to the task at hand. I do not wish to make any strong point on that score, any more than I wish members of

April 1, 1985
Statute Law Amendment Act
the Opposition to use it for their partisan advantage. The reality is that the task of understanding the ramifications of the Charter in light of the existing provisions of our law requires a long, careful and continuing effort by many of us.
In conclusion, I want to report to you, erudite Speaker that you are, that I have been rereading Gordon Allport's classical work on the nature of prejudice, to give some basis for the further work which we will now be doing. He asked whether discrimination and prejudice were facts of the social structure or of the personality structure, and his answer was that indeed they were the results of both.
We are looking here not at the matter of how individuals may in their personalities respond through prejudice in a way that results in discrimination, but at how in the social structure, which includes the laws of this country, the discriminatory provisions, the distinctions that are there, are now, in light of Section 15 of the Charter, eradicated for the betterment of this country and its citizens.

speechtext: Mr. Speaker, what is the opinion of the Hon. Member of the criticism by the Opposition that the Government's approach will force people to go to court to assert their rights under Section 15 of the Charter?

subtopic: STATUTE LAW (CANADIAN CHARTER OF RIGHTS AND FREEDOMS) AMENDMENT ACT MEASURE TO AMEND
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I can say that whether they are from Restigouche or Moose Jaw, the view of Canadians on this will be quite the same. Those comments made by Members, particularly of the Liberal Party, that the approach which the Government is taking will force people to go to the courts to assert their remedies under Section 15 of the Charter is erroneous, misleading and disruptive to the process of this parliamentary committee.
In this country if you can make any statement with assurance, it is the following: nobody in Canada is forced into the courts. Our courts are there as a refuge for people who want to see that in the final analysis the rights and the remedies which they have can be interpreted. That is where they can turn to seek their remedy, if they so wish.
The context in which that has been raised is that the work of the parliamentary committee is now going to review the more complex social and policy issues, the cultural and economic dimensions of many of these issues before us as raised in the booklet Equality Issues in Federal Law. It was said that because this is not all in place and finalized prior to April 17, there will be a period during which people will have to turn to the courts. I just do not buy that. As long as Canada is a country and as long as we have a Charter of Rights, people will be going to the courts to assert their rights, and so it should be.
Everyone can recognize that the great body of complicated issues that are now before us are ones that are properly resting
with the parliamentary committee to deal with them. After all, we are the ones who can legislate. If we decide that mandatory retirement laws are something that should be changed, we can bring in measures to make all the consequent changes that flow from them dealing with the Canadian Pension Plan and other pension plans.
Those are not things the judges of this country can do. That is not their role. Traditionally, it has not been the role of judges in this country to be legislators. That is more the American approach. I believe that every Member of this House, duly elected, recognizing the supremacy of Parliament as the law-making body in our system, would welcome an approach which leaves the greatest amount of control in changing the laws with the duly elected Members representatives of the people.

speechtext: The Hon. Member for York Centre (Mr. Kaplan) told us the other day that the consultation approach of our Government showed that this Government did not take matters seriously. Does the Hon. Member have any comments to make about this statement?

subtopic: STATUTE LAW (CANADIAN CHARTER OF RIGHTS AND FREEDOMS) AMENDMENT ACT MEASURE TO AMEND
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, in my opinion, consultation with the Canadian public is a very important step in the work of our committee. I believe that, for cooperation between the Government and the Canadian people to be successful it has to be expressed in positive terms. I therefore think that the hearings held by our committee will be a very important part of the process. More important, the consultation process will allow us to discuss with the public major problems related to the social, cultural and economic policies on which our laws are based. Another very important fact is that the public will be made more aware of the complexity of the problems we are now discussing. I believe that it is very important and very useful to discuss these problems with the people.

subtopic: STATUTE LAW (CANADIAN CHARTER OF RIGHTS AND FREEDOMS) AMENDMENT ACT MEASURE TO AMEND
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I have a comment plus a question for the Hon. Member for Etobicoke-Lakeshore (Mr. Boyer). He stated that no Bill introduced in this House is the be all and end all. Members from all sides can agree with that. On the other hand, Bill C-27 is a terrible start. Some Bills certainly attempt to address the issue or the area which the Bill tries to cover to find a solution in a more comprehensive, genuine and encompassing way. He also mentioned that perhaps in the backdrop of this Bill, there is a flurry of activity. He mentioned the Equality Now! report with respect to visible minorities, and the Abella Commission. Perhaps he should have mentioned to the Canadian public that those were Liberal initiatives, as was the whole constitutional process and the Charter of Rights.
Perhaps he should also mention to Canadians that most of the objections which came in 1981 and 1982 certainly came
April 1, 1985

from that side of the House and its provincial friends across the country.
The Hon. Member also mentioned the hours and hours that must have gone into amending those 50 federal statutes. He should also mention to Canadians that minority groups spent hours and hours in terms of preparing briefs. Also they spent a lot of money coming to Ottawa to present their views. We should also consider whether it is fair to encumber those individuals or groups throughout the country with having to repeat that performance. We should be asking Canadians whether we should in fact be reinventing the wheel today, April 1, in light of the April 17 deadline.
The Hon. Member talked about September 4 being the date on which this Government was given a clear mandate, a mandate for change. We all recognize what happened on September 4. It is all the more important that it does have the absolute majority, given the political will, that it does have the ability to give Canadians that change. In 1979, the Government acted as if it had a majority. In 1985, it is acting as if it were a minority. Its biggest desire is to be loved by everyone everywhere at the same time without affecting anyone's life, without saying that it is going to take a certain course.
Leadership also means giving direction with the full knowledge that that direction is not acceptable to everybody. By sitting on the fence and not trying to hurt anybody, you are not giving leadership.
I now come to my question. Given the fact that the Hon. Member, through this Bill, is looking at changing federal statutes, 50 pieces of legislation I believe, legislation with which everyone was in agreement, legislation which is purely cosmetic, why did it not tackle the other 950 statutes that need updating? Why stop at 50? Why did the Government not go further? speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I would like to speak to one specific matter which, regrettably, was not covered by Bill C-27 but which, I believe, flows from the Charter of Rights. It is a matter on which urgent action is required and on which initiative has been taken not by the Liberals or Progressive Conservatives but by the New Democratic Party. I am speaking, of course, of the question of political rights or the right to participate in democratic elections and election campaigns of persons who work for the Public Service of Canada and of persons who may work for provincial legislatures.
My focus today is on the federal legislation. This is a matter of real and urgent importance. In fact, I raised this question in the House of Commons today. There are some 120,000 federal employees who live and work in the Province of Ontario. The provincial Government is now entering into an election campaign. Those federal employees were told last February that they were not to take any action which could give rise to the perception that they were acting in a manner which was partisan or which was not impartial during an election campaign. As a consequence, a number of employees, with great trepidation, backed away from participation in the federal election campaign and will in fact back away from participation in the current provincial election campaign. This has happened despite the fact that the Charter of Rights guarantees freedom of speech and freedom of association as fundamental rights, despite the fact that the Charter of Rights, in Section 1, provides for exemptions on a very limited basis, and despite the fact that in Section 15, the Charter of Rights provides equality of rights which should surely ensure that people working for the Government of Canada are given the same kind of treatment in terms of freedom of speech and of association as are other citizens of the country.
This is an urgent matter. My friend, the Hon. Member for Etobicoke-Lakeshore (Mr. Boyer), suggested that no one has to go before the courts. I have been before the courts. I am in fact before the Federal Court of Canada right now in conjunction with four federal Government employees regarding the interference with their rights of association and freedom of speech because of the lack of amendments to Section 32 of the Public Service Employment Act and because of the actions of the Government of Canada as the employer which essentially interfered with basic political rights.
I think it is fair to say that this is an administrative as well as a legislative matter. There has been federal legislation for many years which has tended to interfere with what I believe are the basic democratic rights of federal Government employees just as such legislation exists at the provincial level. Beginning one year ago, guidelines issued by the Public Ser-

April 1, 1985
Statute Law Amendment Act
vice Commission had the effect of stepping up the heat very considerably. The guidelines transferred the enforcement of restrictions on federal employees from the provision in the Public Service Employment Act, which had not been used since 1967 because it required enforcement of a complaint by a political candidate, and no candidate has ever complained, to the internal disciplinary mechanisms of the Public Service. There, as some Hon. Members know, a number of disciplinary actions have been initiated or carried out. People have been suspended, called to account or have had black marks put on their records because of various participations in political life.
The reason I raise this issue now and the reason I raised this question earlier today is that there will possibly be elections later this year in Saskatchewan, Manitoba and the Yukon. There are two election campaigns under way right now. Even if the next federal election does not take place for another three or four years, the question of the rights of people who happen to work for the Government of Canada is one which I believe must be dealt with quite urgently.
I would like to suggest to my hon. friends from all Parties that we should look at the Charter of Rights as hard as we look at Bill C-27. Obviously Bill C-27 is designed to amplify and implement what was intended by the Charter. When looking at the Charter, we find that the Charter itself is rather weak when it comes to the question of democratic rights. Section 3 of the Charter refers to democratic rights and is in fact considerably more limited than I believe it ought to be. It guarantees every citizen of Canada the right to vote in an election for Members of the House of Commons and to be qualified to be a Member of the House of Commons. It also guarantees that no House of Commons will continue for more than five years save under certain narrowly defined emergency circumstances.
It is interesting to compare this with the enormous amount of detail into which the Charter goes with respect to the official languages and with respect to minority language educational rights. In fact, on those two issues, the Charter is almost as detailed as the Bill.
Regarding democratic rights, the Charter is silent on a number of things which I think are extremely important. The Charter does not guarantee citizens of Canada that there will be fair and impartial conduct of elections. It does not guarantee the right of candidates to communicate with their electors and of electors to communicate with their candidates. It will likely be tested in the courts as to whether or not such things as the gerrymandering that is now taking place in British Columbia is in fact forbidden under the equality provisions of Section 15 of the Charter of Rights. If the gerrymandering in that province is not governed by Section 15, I suspect that it will be possible for British Columbia to ensure that the Socreds can have three or four times the number of seats for each vote received compared to the New Democratic Party and not be in violation of the Charter. In other words, we have not thought this particular area through. I would ask my colleagues from all Parties to consider that question very seriously.
Of course, I am speaking initially of the status of people working for the Government of Canada, because it is a fact that promises were made by Progressive Conservative Members when they were running for office last summer and these promises have yet to be implemented. I understand that it takes time to move the wheels of Government and I am hopeful that the promise made by the President of the Treasury Board (Mr. de Cotret) that discussions with the Public Service union will yield a statement very soon will in fact come to pass.
Working under the guarantees which I believe are in the Charter of Rights and Freedoms, I feel that I have no choice but to go to the courts to say that if the citizens of Canada are to have freedom of speech, it should not be denied to a person because of the fact that he happens to work for the Government of Canada, except in so far as Section 1 would apply, and that would be where a restriction is reasonable, where it is proscribed by law, and where it can be demonstrably justified in a free and democratic society.
The jurisprudence limits those restrictions under Section 1 very sharply. The jurisprudence effectively says that one cannot apply a blanket restriction on an entire class of individuals. One may be able to demonstrate that Deputy Ministers and other persons who are providing senior executive services to the Government of Canada might have their political rights restricted or even eliminated entirely because of the nature of their jobs. Surely that restriction should not apply to a truck driver in the Yukon, a secretary working in the Department of National Health and Welfare in Tunney's Pasture, or someone who is a fisheries enforcement officer riding around in a boat somewhere off the coast of Prince Edward Island. Surely that would not be a reasonable kind of restriction.
My problem is that the promise was made by the Government eight months ago as it was coming to office, but we are still to see that promise implemented. The reason I am going to court is that I have regard to the fact that the previous Liberal Government, when in opposition, promised the same thing as the present Government but did not implement it. In fact, there has been more said about the issue of the political rights of federal Government employees in the six months of this Parliament than during the entire four years or four and a half years of the previous Parliament. I would undertake, as the Member for Ottawa Centre who represents a lot of public employees, to continue to raise the issue in Parliament and to urge the Government to act.
I deplore the fact that action is not taken in Bill C-27 and I will take action, if necessary, in the courts if what the Government proposes is not satisfactory. I would argue as well, Mr. Speaker, contrary to my hon. friend, the Hon. Member for Etobicoke-Lakeshore (Mr. Boyer), that it may well be, given the failure of the Government to act, that there is no choice but to go to the courts. There is legislation, I believe, in eight or nine provinces restricting the political rights of provincial
April 1, 1985

public employees. Once those restrictions crack somewhere because of court action, we will see the political rights of all federal and provincial employees enormously expanded. I believe that is very important in view of the guarantees of the Charter of freedom of speech and freedom of association.
1 have to report to you, Mr. Speaker, with regret, that in the court case which I undertook in conjunction with Randy Barnhart, Lynda Camponi, Ken Clavette and Heather Stevens, all employees of the federal Government and members of the Public Service Alliance-this case is in fact being supported financially by the Public Service Alliance-we have had what I think is a terribly retrograde and insensitive response from the Attorney General of Canada (Mr. Crosbie) to the statement of claim we put forward. The gist of that statement is that the restrictions of Section 32 of the Public Service Employment Act on persons who work for the Government of Canada-those are the restrictions which say that if a person works for the Government of Canada, he will not work for a political Party or a candidate in an election-are on partisan political work for a political Party or a candidate in an election. The Attorney General states that the section does not prohibit, limit or infringe upon any person's right to associate with any other person or persons. A person in British Columbia who went to the federal leadership convention of the Leader of the Official Opposition (Mr. Turner) was suspended from working for five days. Public employees in Manitoba working for the Government of Canada were threatened with disciplinary action if they did not withdraw from accepting a delegateship they had been awarded to participate in that particular election campaign. In other words, what the Attorney General seems to be saying is that one can have freedom to associate so long as one does not associate with a political Party. I find that unacceptable, Mr. Speaker.
The Attorney General also argues that entry into or departure from the Public Service of Canada, with all the rights, benefits, obligations and responsibility that entails, are matters of freely exercised choice, and each public servant is subject to the obligations imposed by Section 32 of the said Act only during tenure as an employee. In other words, it is argued that the freedom of speech and of association 250,000 employees of the Government of Canada is not impaired, according to the Charter, because in order to exercise freedom of speech, all they have to do is to quit their job or resign their position in the Public Service. I find that a very unacceptable position, Mr. Speaker.
I believe that during the election campaign the Progressive Conservative Party, at least on the campaign trail, seemed to accept that particular point of view. Those Hon. Members thought that it was an unreasonable kind of restriction. These days, the job market is not particularly good. The Government of Canada covers a wide range of topics, as it has done for a long time. I do not see why someone who is concerned with weights and measures should have to refrain from making a comment about whether Canada should be involved in the U.S. star wars initiative because he happens to be working for the Department of Consumer and Corporate Affairs. That
Statute Law Amendment Act
seems like an unreasonable restriction on his opportunity to comment on a matter which is not only of vital public concern but is of crucial public concern to himself and his children since he, together with everyone else in Ottawa, stands to be blown to smithereens if we get into a nuclear shooting match and the bombs start to fall on our national capital. The Government is casting its nets extraordinarily widely when it says, "Well, you can talk about anything you want, just quit your job".
I think, in a broader sense, Mr. Speaker, that the question of the freedom of individuals to participate in democratic life, without being inhibited by the employer, is something we in this Parliament should look at. We must look at it in part because of the increasing imbalance between power these days between employees and employers, thanks to the high unemployment policy of the Liberal Government prior to September and the policies of the present Progressive Conservative Government. That imbalance gives employers a lot of power over employees. That power can extend to directing an employee to participate, shall we say, in a dinner for the Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) or for some other Progressive Conservative luminary, or perhaps to contribute to the cost of a seat at a fund raising dinner for the Government in power. Perhaps it can even extend to directing an employee that if he wants to keep his job, he had better get out there and work for the local Progressive Conservative candidate, if he knows what is good for him. When a male supervisor harasses a female employee, it is called sexual harassment. But the doors are open to what I might call political harassment. There is no protection against that in terms of our concept of what a person's political rights should be.
I think it is commonly accepted that if a person works for an employer, he owes loyalty to that employer. If a person works for General Motors, that person does not go out after hours and say Chevrolets are lousy cars. If a person works for Beatrice Foods, that person does not tell the public that its yogurt is lousy yogurt. I think that is quite well understood. Likewise, if a person works for Weights and Measures Canada, that person does not go out and criticize the Government's program of metrication. If a person wants to do that, then he either changes his job or resigns. However, Mr. Speaker, I think it would be unconscionable for General Motors to tell an employee that if he chooses to speak out politically after regular working hours, it will censor what he says to make sure that it is consistent with its views as a corporation or, perhaps, with the views of some right-wing shareholders of its company in the United States. I think that would be unconscionable. I believe we have to be aware of that problem, particularly now that the Government of Canada is beginning to put that forward as a position it chooses to take with regard to its employees.
What I am suggesting, Mr. Speaker, is that the question of the political rights of federal Government employees should have been dealt with in Bill C-27. The political rights section or the democratic rights section of the Charter of Rights, is weak. The Charter of Rights suffers from a lack of coherent

and consistent thinking. Perhaps we spent too much time wondering whether we should have a Charter at all and too little time looking at all the areas which should be covered in the Charter.
Failing an amendment to the Charter respecting democratic rights which would broaden the concept of democratic rights along the lines 1 have spoken of, it seems to me it is not fair to require that people test through Section 15, through Section 2, and through the fundamental freedoms sections freedom of speech and freedom of association so that people can involve themselves in political life. I would, therefore, strongly suggest to the Hon. Member for Etobicoke-Lakeshore and to all his colleagues from all Parties who will be taking part in the committee, that even if they cannot make the amendments to Bill C-27, they come back to this House very seriously with recommendations suggesting that further legislation should be embarked upon which would deal not only with the question of the political rights of federal employees. That may be dealt with by other means and in the near future. I suggest that the whole question of democratic rights, in so far as it can be addressed by legislation, flowing from the Charter of Rights in its present form should be addressed by this Parliament during the course of the current session.

Member for Kenora-Rainy River (Mr. Parry) for bringing such a clean and concise resolution before the House to render the necessary death knell to an institution whose time has come and has long since gone.
I know that we, as Members of the Lower House, must contain ourselves and our emotions on this subject. With all decorum possible and appropriate, I will try to address my remarks in the next few moments.
The one Party which is not present to speak to this resolution is the Liberal Party. That is ironic, as the Senate of Canada is the only legislative Chamber in the entire country where that Party has a majority. The movement toward Senate reform really began in 1873 when Liberal Prime Minister Sir Alexander Mackenzie was first elected. He learned to his dismay the uses to which the grand-daddy of our Party, Sir John A. Macdonald, had put the other place. He had applied his political wiles in getting this nation together. It was a difficult task, and part of the expedient which Sir John found necessary was in fact to put in the other place people who', 'April 1, 1985

could only fit there and nowhere else in the political complexion of the country.
Also it is interesting to note, just as a preliminary observation, that indeed there may be a good measure of agreement between representatives of the New Democratic Party and of the Progressive Conservative Party on this movement. One could reflect upon the writings of Gad Horowitz who wrote about the different strains in Canadian political philosophy, how Conservatives come through a philosophical approach which recognizes the organic nature of society, and that indeed socialist Parties spring from the same basic formation and share that organic view of society, that collective perception of how society works. On a few issues such as the one before us, there may indeed be some basis for philosophical agreement between our two Parties. Particularly it is the Conservative instinct to look at the organic growth in this case, perhaps to compare it with a tree and to recognize that the time has come to lop off the moulded branch and by so doing leave the rest of the tree healthy and flourishing.
The movement toward Senate reform in recent years perhaps had its greatest impetus in 1983 when the Trudeau Government brought in a discussion booklet of some 44 pages-and I was just looking at it-outlining its view on Senate reform. It is clear that that discussion paper really represented a synthesis of the many proposals that have come along in recent years to try to breathe new life into a defunct institution. Indeed, I was interested in the comments of my colleagues, the Hon. Member for Edmonton West (Mr. Dorin) reporting on a proposal from Alberta as to how the second Chamber might be revived.
With great respect, all of these proposals strike me as being somewhat analogous to the homestead. Here is the old homestead that we started with. We have come a long way. We are now in a good building with all the modern facilities. But we are still proud of the old log cabin in the back. It was the first structure in which anything happened. We look at that old log cabin and, because of some sense of nostalgia, we do not want to let it go. We wonder what we can do to keep it relevant. We think that maybe we can put in a microwave oven or a television, or possibly a circular driveway. We feel that we might be able to do something to make the old log cabin relevant to the 1980s. Sometimes the best thing that can be done with something that has long outlived its function is simply to let it go the way of history and fade gloriously into the past.
Some of the genesis of these proposals coming from western Canada originated a few years back when there was a feeling of alienation from the Government in the central part of the country. That was quite understandable. It was seen that Senate reform would be a vehicle for bringing western Canadian political imperatives back to the heart of the Government of this nation. That is no longer necessary. It was demonstrated last September 4 that the solution was not institutional change but political change.
Again we have western Canadians fully at the heart and functioning of the Government of Canada. The evidence is the great number of Cabinet Ministers from western Canada, the end of the National Energy Program and its divisive and economically destructive provisions as well as the signing of the Western Accord on energy policy. All of these show that western interests are strongly being represented, that they are being paid attention to and that it is not necessary to make any kind of institutional change such as foisting an elected Senate or any other kind of Senate on this country.
To put it charitably, throughout Canadian history the role of the Senate has been marginal. At sporadic intervals, there were proposals to reform or change the Senate. Those proposals were always met by a couple of arguments. The first was that the Senate provided a sober second thought, that we here in this Chamber, in the hurly-burly and rush of daily debate were too carried up and carried away really to make legislative enactments, but in the other place, the Senators, in the calm and cool interiors, the inner recesses of the time and reflective position, were able to see calmly the errors, omissions, the need for amendation and change, and they would fine tune, with that sober second thought, the legislative enactments.
History has clearly shown that that has not been the case. Without any disrespect, the Senate has served largely as a rubber stamp, except in cases where it has chosen to be merely political and obstreperous.
The other great argument that was given was that the regional representation was manifested in the Senate, as if, by inference, it was not being manifested here in the elected Chamber. My colleague, the Hon. Member for Carleton-Charlotte (Mr. McCain) spoke in defence of the Senate a few moments ago. Nevertheless, in doing so he condemned the maritime Senators for their failure to observe regional interests and to represent effectively the interest of Atlantic Canada. Even from the mouths of those who would support the Senate, come words of condemnation for that second argument that is given to us in support of the Senate.
The sober second thought theory and the regional representation theory just do not wash when analysed in the hard reality of Canadian history. It is at this point that the defenders of the Senate traditionally rush in with the latest and best argument they can muster, that is, that the Senate does some great study, and that the Senate has benefited the nation by bringing forth documents that have painstakingly analysed issues such as poverty and many other topics that are important. The fact is that those studies are done by the staff that is hired by the Senate. There are committees to do that work. Any committee of this House can do likewise. It is the quality of the staff that is reflected directly in those great studies which the Senators from time to time are wont to pull out in their defence.
I disagreed with my colleague, the Hon. Member for Keno-ra-Rainy River, when he alluded to those great studies done by Senators. In fact, it was the late Dr. John Deutsch who had much to do with the great study done there. Mr. Peter Dobell
April 1, 1985', 'of the parliamentary centre, William Hood, who went on to become a Deputy Minister of Finance, and others like that were really responsible for the great studies for which the Senators take claim. With great respect, that should be recognized. Therefore, we can put to an end once and for all that fallacious argument as a defence for maintaining the Senate any longer.
The end of the Senate will allow us to pass through an era where we no longer mislead our friends and allies abroad by the phenomenon whereby they think that when they are in the presence of a Senator they have with them the charismatic presence of someone like a United States Senator, those men of action and power in the United States of America. Our Canadian Senators are just not in the same league.
We have seen what was referred to as a haven for provincial Liberal Party leaders. I think of Senators such as Gildas Molgat, Louis Robichaud, Henry Hicks, Andy Thompson, David Steuart and so on. We are now in an era where the Liberal Party is a Party of yesterday. There are no longer any real provincial Party leaders to be appointed. The Liberal Party is talking of setting up a think-tank, some kind of institute. subtopic: CONSTITUTION ACTS, 1867-1982 SUGGESTED AMENDMENT TO ABOLISH SENATE
CONSTITUTION ACTS, 1867-1982 SUGGESTED AMENDMENT TO ABOLISH SENATE
speechtext:
That, in the opinion of this House, the Constitution Acts, 1867 to 1982, should be amended in order to abolish the Senate, and this House urges that the Senate and the Legislative Assemblies of all provinces pass similar resolutions, and that the Governor General issue a Proclamation under the Great Seal of Canada to that effect.
He said: Mr. Speaker, I rise to present a motion which I am proud and happy to say is very much in the mainstream tradition of my Party. I am hopeful, given some of the statements made in the last election and thereafter on all sides of this House, with the notable exception of the now decimated former Government, that this motion, while it may not lead to the arrival of the moving vans tomorrow, or even perhaps next week, will indeed assist in setting in motion those processes required to rid this country of an institution which once was an embellishment but which has now become an embarrassment.
In speaking today I would like to acknowledge the record of members of my Party, some of whom are no longer in this House, in proposing, promoting and arguing for the abolition of the Senate. I would like to acknowledge the contribution of former Leaders of this Party and its precursors and predecessors, and I would also like to acknowledge the contribution of our present Leader, the Hon. Member for Oshawa (Mr. Broadbent). I will quote briefly from a motion which my Leader sought leave to introduce in the House on March 11. Rather than cite it completely, I think the key phrase in the motion is this:
Whereas the Senate of Canada enjoys legislative powers, but exercises these powers without popular mandate;
If I were asked to make a one-sentence summary of my case for abolition of the Senate, I think those are the words I would choose. The Senate of Canada operates within the Canadian parliamentary framework without a popular mandate.
I would like to take note of the exchange which took place in this House last month in which the Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) was asked by my Leader if he would introduce legislation to abolish the Senate. He replied that he would do so if it were supported by the Leader of the Official Opposition (Mr. Turner). The Prime Minister, of course, in making that tongue-in-cheek request, was acting within his powers but he was not, I think, acting fully in the tradition of this House in seeking the consent of the Leader of the Official Opposition for a legislative measure which, if he, the Prime Minister, and his caucus were fully behind, would require the consent of no other Parties in this House owing to the size of the Government's majority. But, characteristically, the Prime Minister was faster on his feet than his official opponent who did not take him up on the offer. Had he called the Prime Minister's bluff, he could have embarrassed the Government because then they would have had to do something instead of relying merely on rhetoric, wit and evasion to accomplish their objectives within the parliamentary process.
It is not my purpose here today to provide a historical survey or narrative as to the procedures which led to the establishment of the Canadian Senate.

Moreover, I would not want to get into personalities. I understand that there exist rules of mutual respect between members of the House and those of the Senate. And although it might be difficult to deal with either assembly without referring to individuals or general practices, I will try to carry



April 1, 1985

on just the same, and I ask you to correct me if I happen to break the rule.

It matters little, in the context of a resolution to abolish the Senate, what the personal habits, personal worth or strength, or indeed the shortcomings, real, imagined or alleged, of the Members of the other House are. It matters little what the level of their income from their official duties, and I use the term loosely, might be. It matters little what their income from other activities may be, whether it be simply an old age security pension, for which many of them qualify, or indeed pensions and directors' fees and residual income in the hundreds of thousands of dollars which it is alleged pertain to some Members of that other place. I would try to avoid the employment of arguments ad hominem or ad feminem in this respect. While of course those who delight in deductive reasoning can deduce from the general remarks a number of particular allegations, I would ask for their forebearance in that respect. I ask Hon. Members to believe me when I say that I do not intend to offer insult or disrespect to any Member of that other place whose abolition I am advocating.
I would like to discuss the background of second chambers in general. In western constitutional history, bicameralism was originally justified by the need to represent the needs of the aristocratic element of society in a distinctive way within Parliament. The classical theory was expressed by Montesquieu in his The Spirit of Laws. Second chambers have indeed been passionately decried. The objection of Sieyes in the French Revolution is well known: if it contradicts the popular chamber, then it is not democratic. If it merely agrees with the popular chamber, it is then unnecessary. Harold Laskey said that anyone who examines the nature and history of second chambers in general will discover that their main purpose is at least to delay and, if possible, to prevent the disturbance of the status quo. They are in fact part of the general tactics of conservatism. I would point out that the conservatism instanced is of the small "c" variety, and I would acknowledge that many of my friends from the Conservative caucus also find the continued existence of the Senate at variance with the fundamental principles of democracy.
Since World War II second chambers have been abolished in Demark, Sweden and New Zealand, as well as in the Province of Quebec in 1968, which removed the last provincial second chamber from the Canadian scene. According to a survey carried out a decade ago, unicameralism, the function of a single elected chamber, prevails in 84 countries, and bicameralism, two chambers, in only 55.
The faults of the institution were in my Leader's remarks as being those of an institution which was established in an immature phase of Canadian democracy, a phase which has long since passed. The Senate was modelled, as were many Canadian institutions, on a British constitutional model. It is hardly radical to say that in Canada in 1985 we are at a very different phase of our development than we were in 1867 when we still functioned very much as an appendage of the mother country, in this case Great Britain. Canada's Senate was
The Senate
modelled on the House of Lords. The principle of the House of Lords in the British system, though not explicitly stated, was to provide a break for the powerful, the privileged, and the landed on the initiatives of the democratic society which they had historically governed. Second chambers were considered necessary to protect business and commercial interests from the workings of popular government.
In its concept and operation the Senate is neither regionally representative in the sense we understand today, nor is it democratic. It is in fact, as a former Member of this place and the next Premier of Ontario stated, "an undemocratic institution working at the heart of democratic government". I refer, of course, to an article by Bob Rae.
During its history the Senate has served mainly as a tool of patronage for the Party of power and as such has attracted continued criticism from my Party. It is, in a sense, a sort of escape hatch, a promotion alley, or a retirement institution for the two major Parties which have held the Government of this country over the last 117 years. It is, I believe, discredited in the eyes of the public. Of course, we must consider that simply by abolishing the Senate we will not necessarily accomplish an increase in public esteem for the House of Commons. We must look to ourselves to accomplish that.
It is difficult for me to see how any authentically Canadian institution could be established which would fulfil, in a democratic way and context, the role that the Senate is presently supposed to fill. It is not hard to understand that, since the governing elite of the Liberal and Progressive Conservative Parties are the potential candidates in this cash for life bonanza, they too will find it difficult to be driving forces behind a move for reform. It is, therefore, all the more commendable that there are some members of the Government Party who are prepared to speak in favour of this Bill.
The faults of usage of the Senate are indeed legion. The Hon. Member for Kamloops-Shuswap (Mr. Riis) referred to it as a home for hacks, flacks, and bagmen. I had to question why he was less than all-encompassing and did not mention bagwomen, or indeed why he was so generous. It is a prime instrument of patronage. It is a way of keeping retired politicians in the style to which they have become accustomed. I think the real question is why they should have become accustomed to such a high style in the first place, rather than why such a style should not be continued. It has been used as a repository for fired Ministers. The well-known term is "kicked upstairs".
I think the most obnoxious abuse of the Senate over the last few years has been that pioneered by the late, totally unlamented, ancien regime and its Leader, in that they made the Senate into a holding tank for their campaign teams. I am pleased to say, though I wish the proportions had been different, that the Canadian people decisively repudiated that back-slapping, basically venal and mercenary approach in the last election. I think it does great credit to the people of Canada that they did see through it.

April 1, 1985
The Senate
1 would contrast the situation in our provinces and municipalities, which have no second chamber, with that in the federal Government and state my belief that, in the eyes of most Canadians, municipal and provincial Governments function in a more efficient fashion and relate better to the people they represent than does the federal Government. It is my belief that approximately 85 per cent of the legislation in Canada, including provincial legislation and municipal by-laws, goes through without benefit of the attention of a second chamber. My belief is that that legislation is not evidently or markedly inferior for the fact of being considered only by a single chamber.
While the Senate has no direct contact with money Bills, it is nevertheless true that approximately 85 per cent of the decision on spending, that which is subject to examination and not mandatory by legislation or program, goes through the provincial and municipal legislatures and councils.
The prime functions of government are three, Mr. Speaker. They are to establish laws, to spend money on purposes seen as legitimate, and to establish and promote a political ethos, ethic or culture within the country and society. I believe that Canada is not advantaged or benefited in any of those three prime purposes by the presence and intervention of the Senate.
In closing, Mr. Speaker, lest it be said that I did not have a good word for the Senate, I would say that we do acknowledge that there have been some valuable reports and long-term studies carried out by that institution in the last few years. They have been thought-provoking, intelligent, and, in many cases, marked by sound analysis and sound recommendations. In acknowledging that small praise we must turn to the overwhelming drawbacks of this institution, not the least of which is money. There is $27 million budgeted for 1985-86. I feel that we must acknowledge that the functions which it carries out could be carried out more effectively, efficiently, economically, and with less offence to the people and public of Canada, by the hiring of additional parliamentary draftsmen, additional staff for paliamentary committees, and even by the Members themselves.
The Senate of Canada is an idea whose time has passed, Mr. Speaker. We have the opportunity in this Parliament to make it what it truly deserves to be, a part of history. I hope we will not let that opportunity pass.
