Mr. Speaker, the Hon. Member for Kenora-Rainy River (Mr. Parry) did point out that there has been some good work done in the Senate. For that I commend him. With regard to the balance of his remarks, 1 suggest that a little more study and a little more analysis of what must be done by the Government of Canada should reveal to him that perhaps the House of Commons, in some regards, is already overloaded. Perhaps there is a very good reason, as I believe there to be, to divide an element of that load between the upper Chamber and the House of Commons.
I suppose if the Senate has a bad name, it is because it has been abused by some Prime Ministers of the past, and particularly by the Prime Minister who was most recently removed from office. It was abused when legislation was passed to it at three o'clock in the afternoon with orders that that legislation must be back for Royal Assent by five o'clock at the latest. It must not keep the House of Commons waiting. That certainly deprived that Chamber of any opportunity to give any thought, let alone sober second thought, to the performance of the House of Commons.
Today we discussed a Bill dealing with the Constitution. It is an example of an issue that would have benefited from some extended sober second thought. If that had taken place earlier, it would not have been necessary to debate the Bill which was before us today and which must be passed in order to accommodate the Constitution. The Constitution was not properly planned, and the Senators were capable of doing that study.

subtopic: CONSTITUTION ACTS, 1867-1982 SUGGESTED AMENDMENT TO ABOLISH SENATE
speechtext: They didn't do it.

subtopic: CONSTITUTION ACTS, 1867-1982 SUGGESTED AMENDMENT TO ABOLISH SENATE
speechtext:
They did not have the time to do it. Members will know that the constitutional legislation was introduced to the House with a time limit attached to it. It was not here for in-depth consideration and the subject matter was not placed before the committee for the purpose of hearing recommendations from the people. It was there purely for show.
The committee was shown the frailties which existed in constitutions in other jurisdictions. It heard recommendations for a constitution that would not make the court the legislator while depriving the House of Commons of its legislative capabilities. Some of those recommendations came from some Members of the other place.
I suggest that the House of Commons is already overburdened with work. There are complaints from Members of all Parties about inadequate time for debate and that the committees of the House do not have the time, under the present structure, to give proper consideration to all the items that are placed before it. Therefore, I suggest that there is more reason today for a bicameral government than ever before. I realize that this view conflicts with that of many Members from all Parties. I understand that the reputation of the Senate has been shaped not only by its historic performance but also by the abuse it has suffered from Governments that did not want sober second thought or interference with their own legislative agenda.
I submit that there is no better example of the abuse of the present structure as occasionally imposed upon the House than the filibuster undertaken by the former Deputy Prime Minister of Canada against the budgetary requirements of Canada which occurred at a very inopportune moment. He perpetrated another another disfavour to the Senate to which he was appointed with the full knowledge of the consequence of the extension of that debate.
As the Member for Kenora-Rainy River (Mr. Parry) said, the Agriculture Committee of the Senate has provided Canada with a study of soil erosion and deterioration that 1 believe other jurisdictions will want to examine carefully. It is in that
April 1, 1985

way, in addition to the study of a government's legislative program, that the Senate should function.
There is room for change and a review of the method of appointments. There may be room for change in the duration of an appointment, all of which may be very constructive for an improved Senate. However, I believe the Senate should exist.
In the time I have been here since 1972, the work-load of a Member of Parliament has more than doubled. There is no longer enough time for Members of the House of Commons to fulfill their committee responsibilities and constituency responsibilities within the framework in which we now exist. I believe there is room for the Senate within that structure.
Let us consider one situation that was addressed during the last election campaign. It concerns the regulatory structure that is imposed upon Canada. During the last ten years, government Departments have had what is essentially a blank cheque to make regulations to govern, not necessarily by law but by their regulatory capability. I believe that the Senate could undertake to remove some of those regulations that are imposed by that departmental structure. The committee which presently reviews these regulations has been ineffective in the past and is unlikely to have enough time to study all the regulations now in place or being proposed. Furthermore, my experience with that committee from attending its meetings indicates that it does not have the time to understand the consequences of the regulations that are made. I believe this is a function which the Senate could undertake very well.
Let me say that I would abhor an elected Senate. An elected Senate would increase the number of elections to be held in Canada. Moreover, if there were to be a Senate election shortly after a national election, historical evidence would suggest that the Senate would be politically opposite to the Government of the day. That is the case at the moment, but it will be corrected in time. Nothing could be more confusing or condemnatory than an elected Senate opposing the government of the day and the policies on which it was elected.
While the Senate has its weaknesses and there is room for change, there is no room for abolition. It would be acceptable to review Senate appointments and its relationship to the Government.
According to the Constitution, the purpose of Senate appointments is to provide regional representation. I condemn those Senators from Atlantic Canada who have failed to recognize their regional responsibility, regardless of Party, affiliation. Not only Altantic Canada has suffered seriously but other regions have equally suffered because senators have put their political affiliation ahead of the well-being of their region. If there is a reason to condemn the Senate, that is it. We saw evidence of that irresponsibility in the Senate in the last few weeks. No one should be appointed to the Senate without recognizing his or her regional responsibilities. Under those circumstances, I believe the Government would consider legislative amendments when they impact a particular region unfavourably.
The Senate
While the Senate may need some redirection, I believe it is necessary. I am a strong proponent of the bicameral system, particularly in view of the load that Members of the House must carry.

speechtext:
I am sorry, Mr. Speaker. I will refrain from those kinds of remarks. Today, I essentially wanted to draw the attention of the House to a very recent report on Senate reform by the Alberta Legislature Select Special Committee on Senate Reform, released on March 22. Before I summarize the report's main recommendations, let me mention that the report demonstrates a strong belief in the need for and potential value of a reformed Senate. In the words of the report, the Alberta Legislative Assembly
-rose to the challenge to study Senate reform because of the feelings of Albertans toward the Senate of Canada.
The report goes on:
In the last few years Albertans have experienced feelings of alienation unmatched in past decades of Confederation. These heightened feelings of alienation resulted primarily from the contentious energy and constitutional discussions of the past few years with the former government in Ottawa. Albertans reacted vigorously against a federal government which was clearly insensitive to this province's needs.
Of course, Mr. Speaker, the Party in government in Ottawa is no longer the same. However, the Alberta Committee does not believe that the results of last year's election made Senate reform unnecessary.
The recommendations of the committee follow what has come to be known, particularly in Alberta, as the "Triple-E" model for a reformed Senate. According to the report, the Senate should be directly elected, with each province represented by an equal number of Senators. In addition, "Senators should have powers which would allow them to be effective in providing the regional voice envisioned by the Fathers of Confederation".

April 1, 1985
The Senate
The principal purpose of the reformed Senate envisaged by the Alberta Committee would be "to represent the regions in the federal decision-making process". The report notes, however, that the term "region" should be synonymous with the term province. The Committee believes the role of sober second thought should be the Senate's second most important function. I suggest it is not as relevant today because communication is almost instantaneous as opposed to what we might have seen in the 1800s or 1900s when communication was by pony express. Unlike the Alberta Government's 1982 discussion paper, the report does not propose that the Senate have an intergovernmental role. On this count, the report is very clear when it states:
To give the directly elected Canadian Senate even limited authority in the area of intergovernmental negotiations could complicate and blur the Canadian governmental process rather than encourage smooth intergovernmental negotiations.
A unique feature of the report is its call that the election be held during provincial elections. Senators would be elected during provincial elections for terms equal to the life of two legislatures, according to the first-past-the-post system now used for this House and other elected legislatures in Canada. Senators' terms would be staggered, that is, one-half would be elected during each provincial election. Senators would represent the province as a whole, as do American and Australian Senators. They would not represent a particular district within a province, as, for example, the report of the Special Joint Committee recommended a little over a year ago.
I have already noted that the Alberta Committee proposes equal provincial representation in the reformed Senate. I should add that each province would have six Senators and the Territories two each, for a total membership of 64.
As for the powers of the reformed Senate, the report makes the following general comment:
In Canada today, the Senate possesses power but does not exercise it because Members and non-Members regard it as lacking credibility. As a result, Canadians are witnessing an imbalance in the federal system of government. The Committee strongly recommends that a reformed Senate must be provided with "power" in order to live up to its purposes.
More specifically, the Alberta Committee recommends that the Senate have the power to initiate all legislation except money or taxation Bills; that the Senate have the power to amend any Bill, after which the House of Commons would consider the amendment; that the Senate retain the existing 180-day suspensive veto over constitutional amendments; that the Senate have the power to veto any Bill except a supply Bill; that the House of Commons have the power to override a Senate veto of money or taxation Bills by a simple majority; that the House of Commons be able to override any Senate veto or amendment of a Bill, other than a money or taxation Bill, by a vote that is greater in percentage terms than the Senate's vote to amend; that the Senate vote on a money or taxation Bill within 90 days and on other Bills within 180 days after passage by the House of Commons; that non-military treaties be subject to Senate ratification; and that all changes affecting the French and English languages be subject to a double majority veto, that is, a majority of all Senators
combined with a majority of French-speaking Senators or English-speaking Senators, depending on the issue.
The final set of recommendations in the Alberta Committee's report concerns the Senate's internal organization. It is clear that the main purpose of those recommendations is to reduce the influence of political Parties in a reformed Senate. In the words of the report:
The Committee noted an absence of recommendations in other reports and studies on how the internal organizational structure of the Senate might be set in order to reduce potential party influence of Senators .. . The Committee recognizes that it would be extremely difficult, if not impossible, to eliminate party influence over Senators. However, changes can be made to the internal organizational structure which will go a long way towards lessening this influence.
The specific changes proposed in the report are the following: that the traditional opposition and government roles in the current Senate be abolished, including the positions of Government Leader and Opposition Leader; that Senators be seated in provincial delegations, regardless of Party affiliation; that each provincial delegation select from its membership a chairman who should sit at the pleasure of the provincial delegation; that the Speaker be elected by a majority of the Senate at a specified time every four years, and that there be a provision for the Senate, at any time, to initiate an election of the Speaker by a two-thirds vote; that the ten provincial chairmen, headed by the Speaker of the Senate, constitute a Senate Executive Council; and that the Senate Executive Council determine the order of business of the Senate and appoint committee chairmen and committee members. In addition, the Committee recommended that the determination of whether a Bill is or is not a money or taxation Bill be carried out by joint agreement of the Speakers of the House of Commons and the Senate; that Senate Executive Council members receive remuneration and staff assistance in addition to that received by other Senators; and that Senators not be eligible for appointments to Cabinet. This would keep them out of the difficulty of being in a situation where they have to assume collective responsibility for the Government.
I would simply say that, in my own view, the Select Committee of the Alberta Legislative Assembly should be given a good deal of credit for its thorough study. I believe its report will be discussed widely, both in Alberta and at the national level, and will be a useful contribution to the examination of the future of the Canadian Senate.
I would like to examine quickly two of the proposals. The first is, if we consider the purpose of the Senate, that we add two additional proposes. First, that the Senate try to take a longer term view, with longer term objectives in a less partisan way. Second, that the Senate have the opportunity to review federal appointments which have significant regional impact.
Finally, I would like to suggest that while it has been suggested in the report that the Senate should be elected, I think we should consider that election might not necessarily be essential. I believe the call for election has come recently because of the current situation and the view of the public with regard to the Senate. If the Senate were reorganized, we might look at some of the other options that have been put forward for appointment, either federal appointments, provincial
April 1, 1985

appointments, a selection by one government or the other of a short list presented by the other government, or some combination of these factors. Elections, Mr. Speaker, have their pitfalls. One of them is that there will continue to be a short-term partisan view if it were necessary to seek re-election even for a second term. Beyond that I would suggest that with the elected requirement, people in the Senate would be looking, even if they were not personally seeking re-election, to try to present the views of their Party to ensure that a member of their Party was elected later. I do not think we would be able to keep partisan politics out of it.
In any event, I just wanted to try to outline some of those viewpoints. I think it is a good report, I think we should examine it and other reports that undoubtedly will be coming forward, but I do endorse the Hon. Member for Kenora-Rainy River's (Mr. Parry) stand that the way to get the ball rolling might be to call initially for abolition of the current Senate.

Mr. Speaker, I will speak very briefly on the motion before us because I would like to see it go to committee to be dealt with and become law. I should like to begin by acknowledging the contribution of the Hon. Member opposite. He agrees with abolition. He took the position which our Leader took, that abolishing the undemocratic and non-representative Senate which exists today would really open the door to various possibilities for the creation of another institution that could be truly representative of Canadians. The abolition of the Senate as it exists today should not in any way cut off any options of Canadians to have a second chamber that represents regional interests or minority interests, and it should have a reasonable structure to it.
My comments will not have much to do with the Senate itself, as I do not want to be disrespectful of the other place. My comments will not really be aimed at it but at how it has been used, particularly by Prime Ministers. They have used the Senate as their personal plaything, as a place in which to put old political war-horses. That is an abuse of the Senate and is not the fault of the institution itself. Even our new Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) recognizes that the Senate has been abused and used by Prime Ministers as a place of patronage. He recognizes it more than anyone else. During the last election campaign, he very effectively condemned the Liberals for their flood of patronage appointments, including those to the Senate. He pointed out how wrong and how abusive that was of the institution, of the public and of the powers of the Prime Minister.
It is sad that once the hon. gentleman assumed office he did not go down a new road or find non-partisan ways of making appointments. He started by making a few good appointments, such as that of Stephen Lewis. That was an excellent appointment. He will do a good job at the United Nations for Canadians. Unfortunately, the Prime Minister is hiding behind that good appointment and other good ones. He is using them as a smoke-screen for the patronage appointments in which he has been indulging to an extent unheard of in Canadian
The Senate
history. The Prime Minister has achieved a new record of the number of patronage appointments.

speechtext:
I am sure that is true. Quite naturally the Prime Minister was somewhat teed off with the Senate when it held up his money Bill, and when he returned to the House of Commons he said that he would reform the other place. Unfortunately he did not bring forward any specific reform proposals. However, he has let it be known that he intends to limit the powers of the other place.
Our fear is that he will limit the powers of the other place but preserve it as a place in which to put old political war-horses, that he will preserve it as a patronage tool. If he had good intentions with regard to the Senate, if he wanted to change the method of appointment and make it non-partisan, he should have held off on any appointments to that place until he had brought forward his reform package to the House of Commons. He failed to do that.
As I said, the Senate has been much abused. We could start all over by abolishing it now. If we want a second chamber, we could have some real negotiations as to what it could be, what functions it could serve, how it could acquire its political legitimacy and what interests it could represent. It is not good enough to treat the Senate as a patronage tool, nor is it good enough to simply limit its powers so that it can continue to play that role in Canadian history.
I hope Hon. Members will adopt the resolution of my colleague. If we want a second chamber, we should approach the matter with a clean slate, as the Hon. Member opposite said.

subtopic: CONSTITUTION ACTS, 1867-1982 SUGGESTED AMENDMENT TO ABOLISH SENATE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am delighted to have a few moments in which to participate in this debate. I applaud the Hon. Member for Kenora-Rainy River (Mr. Parry) for bringing such a clean and concise resolution before the House to render the necessary death knell to an institution whose time has come and has long since gone.
I know that we, as Members of the Lower House, must contain ourselves and our emotions on this subject. I know we must always speak with respect for the Senate or, as we are constrained in this Chamber, must refer to it as the other place. With all decorum possible and appropriate, I will try to address my remarks in the next few moments.
The one Party which is not present to speak to this resolution is the Liberal Party. That is ironic, as the Senate of Canada is the only legislative Chamber in the entire country where that Party has a majority. The movement toward Senate reform really began in 1873 when Liberal Prime Minister Sir Alexander Mackenzie was first elected. He learned to his dismay the uses to which the grand-daddy of our Party, Sir John A. Macdonald, had put the other place. He had applied his political wiles in getting this nation together. It was a difficult task, and part of the expedient which Sir John found necessary was in fact to put in the other place people who

April 1, 1985
The Senate
could only fit there and nowhere else in the political complexion of the country.
Also it is interesting to note, just as a preliminary observation, that indeed there may be a good measure of agreement between representatives of the New Democratic Party and of the Progressive Conservative Party on this movement. One could reflect upon the writings of Gad Horowitz who wrote about the different strains in Canadian political philosophy, how Conservatives come through a philosophical approach which recognizes the organic nature of society, and that indeed socialist Parties spring from the same basic formation and share that organic view of society, that collective perception of how society works. On a few issues such as the one before us, there may indeed be some basis for philosophical agreement between our two Parties. Particularly it is the Conservative instinct to look at the organic growth in this case, perhaps to compare it with a tree and to recognize that the time has come to lop off the moulded branch and by so doing leave the rest of the tree healthy and flourishing.
The movement toward Senate reform in recent years perhaps had its greatest impetus in 1983 when the Trudeau Government brought in a discussion booklet of some 44 pages-and I was just looking at it-outlining its view on Senate reform. It is clear that that discussion paper really represented a synthesis of the many proposals that have come along in recent years to try to breathe new life into a defunct institution. Indeed, I was interested in the comments of my colleagues, the Hon. Member for Edmonton West (Mr. Dorin) reporting on a proposal from Alberta as to how the second Chamber might be revived.
With great respect, all of these proposals strike me as being somewhat analogous to the homestead. Here is the old homestead that we started with. We have come a long way. We are now in a good building with all the modern facilities. But we are still proud of the old log cabin in the back. It was the first structure in which anything happened. We look at that old log cabin and, because of some sense of nostalgia, we do not want to let it go. We wonder what we can do to keep it relevant. We think that maybe we can put in a microwave oven or a television, or possibly a circular driveway. We feel that we might be able to do something to make the old log cabin relevant to the 1980s. Sometimes the best thing that can be done with something that has long outlived its function is simply to let it go the way of history and fade gloriously into the past.
Some of the genesis of these proposals coming from western Canada originated a few years back when there was a feeling of alienation from the Government in the central part of the country. That was quite understandable. It was seen that Senate reform would be a vehicle for bringing western Canadian political imperatives back to the heart of the Government of this nation. That is no longer necessary. It was demonstrated last September 4 that the solution was not institutional change but political change.
Again we have western Canadians fully at the heart and functioning of the Government of Canada. The evidence is the great number of Cabinet Ministers from western Canada, the end of the National Energy Program and its divisive and economically destructive provisions as well as the signing of the Western Accord on energy policy. All of these show that western interests are strongly being represented, that they are being paid attention to and that it is not necessary to make any kind of institutional change such as foisting an elected Senate or any other kind of Senate on this country.
To put it charitably, throughout Canadian history the role of the Senate has been marginal. At sporadic intervals, there were proposals to reform or change the Senate. Those proposals were always met by a couple of arguments. The first was that the Senate provided a sober second thought, that we here in this Chamber, in the hurly-burly and rush of daily debate were too carried up and carried away really to make legislative enactments, but in the other place, the Senators, in the calm and cool interiors, the inner recesses of the time and reflective position, were able to see calmly the errors, omissions, the need for amendation and change, and they would fine tune, with that sober second thought, the legislative enactments.
History has clearly shown that that has not been the case. Without any disrespect, the Senate has served largely as a rubber stamp, except in cases where it has chosen to be merely political and obstreperous.
The other great argument that was given was that the regional representation was manifested in the Senate, as if, by inference, it was not being manifested here in the elected Chamber. My colleague, the Hon. Member for Carleton-Charlotte (Mr. McCain) spoke in defence of the Senate a few moments ago. Nevertheless, in doing so he condemned the maritime Senators for their failure to observe regional interests and to represent effectively the interest of Atlantic Canada. Even from the mouths of those who would support the Senate, come words of condemnation for that second argument that is given to us in support of the Senate.
The sober second thought theory and the regional representation theory just do not wash when analysed in the hard reality of Canadian history. It is at this point that the defenders of the Senate traditionally rush in with the latest and best argument they can muster, that is, that the Senate does some great study, and that the Senate has benefited the nation by bringing forth documents that have painstakingly analysed issues such as poverty and many other topics that are important. The fact is that those studies are done by the staff that is hired by the Senate. There are committees to do that work. Any committee of this House can do likewise. It is the quality of the staff that is reflected directly in those great studies which the Senators from time to time are wont to pull out in their defence.
I disagreed with my colleague, the Hon. Member for Keno-ra-Rainy River, when he alluded to those great studies done by Senators. In fact, it was the late Dr. John Deutsch who had much to do with the great study done there. Mr. Peter Dobell
April 1, 1985

of the parliamentary centre, William Hood, who went on to become a Deputy Minister of Finance, and others like that were really responsible for the great studies for which the Senators take claim. With great respect, that should be recognized. Therefore, we can put to an end once and for all that fallacious argument as a defence for maintaining the Senate any longer.
The end of the Senate will allow us to pass through an era where we no longer mislead our friends and allies abroad by the phenomenon whereby they think that when they are in the presence of a Senator they have with them the charismatic presence of someone like a United States Senator, those men of action and power in the United States of America. Our Canadian Senators are just not in the same league.
We have seen what was referred to as a haven for provincial Liberal Party leaders. I think of Senators such as Gildas Molgat, Louis Robichaud, Henry Hicks, Andy Thompson, David Steuart and so on. We are now in an era where the Liberal Party is a Party of yesterday. There are no longer any real provincial Party leaders to be appointed. The Liberal Party is talking of setting up a think-tank, some kind of institute. That would be a great place, when we abolish the Senate, to which those great thinkers of the Liberal Party, Senators Pitfield and Kirby, can go. Their role to the nation would not be denied. They will be able to carry on function as part of the Liberal think-tank.
The notion of the Senate being integral to the system of Government is erroneous. It may indeed be central to our system of Party Government, but even there we can render a great service to the Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) who has to make the appointments to the Senate. It is no secret or mystery around here that for every one person appointed to the Senate, 30, yea, 40, possibly 50 others are left in a state of disconsolateness and shock.
I know a former Liberal Member who represented Sault Ste. Marie. He had been directly and expressly promised by a former Prime Minister, Mr. Pearson, that he would go to his great reward in the other place. It never happened. If we were to abolish the Senate, we would render a great service by bringing to an end the house of broken promises and shattered dreams.
These are but a few of the reasons that I think it is important, indeed incumbent upon us to be supportive of the move to abolish the Senate. If the Senate we must have, 1 would see a properly appointed Senate on the same basis that we appoint our judges. That would be far preferable to an elected Senate.

Mr. Speaker, I rise under the provisions of Standing Order 45. In the House on March 27, I asked the Hon. Minister of Employment and Immigration (Miss MacDonald) about the Ernst Zundel case. Since Mr. Zundel had been sentenced to 15 months, I asked how a determination would be made about whether or not to begin deportation proceedings. The Minister mentioned that an inquiry had begun that very day.
I would like to make a few comments about this most serious situation because we are dealing with the entire climate of freedom and goodwill in this country. I understand that the review to which the Minister referred is relatively automatic if a person is sentenced to six or more months' imprisonment or if a person is convicted of a crime that has a maximum penalty of at least five years' imprisonment.
Mr. Zundel was convicted under Criminal Code Section 177 which indicates that it is a criminal offence to knowingly-and that is the operative word-publish a false statement that causes or is likely to cause injury or mischief to a public interest. I think there is something wrong when a situation as serious as this must be dealt with under an almost obscure law such as this one. We need more meaningful laws that deal more directly with a matter as serious as the Zundel case.
Mr. Zundel arrived in this country some 27 years ago. He still enjoys landed immigrant status. It is clear from what has been said that he is not contrite in any way. I will likely hear from the Parliamentary Secretary about just how long these proceedings may be dragged out, but normally one of the things we look for is the assurance of an attitude of rehabilitation. To be very frank about it, I do not see anything even approaching that in this case.
I have made the point that we are using the wrong law for a case like this. One of the real tragedies is that the approach taken in this case ended up with the victims on trial and not the perpetrator. I have spoken out on this on a number of occasions. On March 3, I was at a Toronto regional annual meeting of the B'nai, B'rith held at a synagogue in central Toronto. On Sunday, March 10, along with a number of other colleagues I attended a service for the Jewish war veterans, and I had the opportunity to express views at that time. On the same day I attended a meeting at the O'Keefe Centre where about 5,000 people from the Jewish community got together to think, talk and pray about this most regrettable situation that was allowed to develop in this country. At the afternoon session, Mr. Speaker, we visited with the Jewish war veterans

April 1, 1985

and had a special service. Mr. Ernst Koch, the Consulate General from West Germany, was present. In the course of his remarks he said:
The issue of redress of wrongs committed during Germany's nazi regime has been dealt with.
It is clear from his remarks-and I believe it took a lot of courage and dignity for that gentleman to attend that particular service-that Mr. Zundel himself may not be welcome back in Germany itself. I would just like to quote a couple of comments from The Gazette of March 27, 1985:
Canada would be a better place wihtout Ernst Zundel.
Mr. Zundel fancies himself a martyr on behalf of free speech, but he is a sorry example of the values upon which this country is founded.
The Jewish community itself, as you well know, Mr. Speaker, was divided on the issue of whether further action should have been taken. Since the action was initiated by Mrs. Sabrena Citron, and since Mr. Zundel has now been sentenced, I believe it is largely the view of the Community that this gentleman should be dealt with effectively and quickly, and not over what I would call a protracted period of time.
I visited Israel in January of this year, and I spent an hour and a half with a group at Yad Vashem. Anyone with any sensitivity would know that the holocaust did indeed happen. I would ask the Parliamentary Secretary if there are any precedents to deal more expeditiously with a situation like this? How many legat steps are there? How can we deal with this man in a strong yet thoughtful way? We all pride ourselves on our freedom in this country. However, there are extremes and they must be dealt with.

speakeroldname: Mr. Jean-Guy Hudon (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of Employment and Immigration):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Employment and Immigration
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I should like to complete the reply which the Minister of Employment and Immigration (Miss MacDonald) made to the Hon. Member for Don Valley East (Mr. Attewell) on March 27, 1985.
A report pursuant to the Immigration Act was prepared by an immigration officer and submitted to the Deputy Minister of Employment and Immigration on March 26, 1985, following the reception on that date of a certificate of conviction to the effect that Mr. Zundel had been sentenced to 15 months in jail.
As early as March 27, upon the initiative of the Minister of Employment and Immigration, the Deputy Minister issued an instruction to a senior immigration officer to carry out an inquiry pursuant to Section 27(3) of the Act. The proper instructions were given to the senior immigration officer the next day. This senior officer will initiate the inquiry shortly. A notice of inquiry will be sent to Mr. Zundel. He will be advised of his right to be represented by a legal counsel or any other person he should deem qualified.
The inquiry will be conducted by an adjudicator in the presence of Mr. Zundel and his counsel. The duration of the inquiry may vary, depending on the legal recourse Mr. Zundel might seek, including the adjournment he might ask for to prepare his case, motions to the Federal Court and so on. During the inquiry and before the adjudicator should render his decision, Mr. Zundel may seek refugee status. The processing of such an application could take as much as a year.
Should a deportation order be issued against Mr. Zundel, he would be entitled, as a permanent resident, to appeal to the Appeal Board of Immigration. This could take six months. Mr. Zundel could also appeal to the Federal Appeal Court or the Supreme Court of Canada of the decision rendered by the adjudicator or the Appeal Board of Immigration, which would require another year.

Mr. Speaker, on March 20 I rose in my place and asked a question of the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Wise) concerning his attempts to implement a cost recovery program against farmers for the inspection services traditionally performed at Agriculture Canada. This change came about because of the economic statement of November 8 when the Minister of Finance (Mr. Wilson) announced that the budget for Agriculture Canada would be cut by some $65 million. Some $23 million of those cuts would be in inspection services. The Department would then be charging farmers an additional $33 million for the inspection services eliminated because of the $23 million cut.
I suppose one could ask where is the efficiency of getting the Government out of inspection services since the new services are obviously going to cost at least $10 million more. However, the focus of my questions on March 20 had to do with the fact which had come to light that the Minister knew that the ultimate result would be to inflict harm on Canadian farmers, not only by increasing the operating costs of a whole industry, which has essentially had its net income frozen for the last 10 years at about $3.5 billion, but in addition, and this is even more damning evidence as the Minister knew this quite clearly from his briefing notes, this particular set of proposals would reduce the output of grain in this country. Yet, despite that, he deliberately went ahead with the proposals to reduce the output of farm products in this country.
The Minister knew from his briefing notes that a great many small plants processing hogs, cattle, and sheep in this country would not be able to continue operation under the new proposals as many of them could not afford to stay in business with the daily total charge of $125 for inspection. A lot of small towns and villages have processing or slaughtering plants which process a few dozen animals. This would increase their costs of inspection per animal far beyond anything their
April 1, 1985

competition has to put up with in the larger centres. It would eventually push these people out of business. Jobs would be lost in these small communities, and a service which people in these small communities take advantage of would disappear.
The Minister in responding tried to pretend that what we had heard was not an economic statement but simply a proposal to begin negotiations. That is so much claptrap. It is very clear that the Minister of Finance intends to achieve a saving of $65 million in the expenditures of the Department of Agriculture, and has every intention of collecting $33 million in so-called cost-recovery, but which is simply an extra tax on agricultural production. There is nothing there to negotiate, yet the Minister gives the impression that he is prepared to do some negotiating.
His own briefing notes point out that they should work with the industry towards agreement on these proposals. While remaining firm on questions of policy, they can be flexible as to the mechanics of the application. For example, the industry may have valid reasons for preferring a particular basis of payment on recovery, such as a per hour or per head or per lot basis. The notes also said they can be flexible regarding who in future might perform the work or how it might be done. For example, an industry group might suggest that at some future date they provide the service themselves. The nature of the meetings should be informative and consultative. Under no circumstances should there be confrontation. They say they should emphasize that fees are based on the nature and cost of each program. Avoid industry to industry or program to program comparisons.
They were very careful to make certain, Mr. Speaker, that the proposed fee charges were not generally known. Each industry got its specific proposal. They knew they were being charged 10 or 15 times more than had been the practice in the past, but they did not know how they stacked up against other sectors in the industry. The horticulture industry found out what its proposed charges will be; the Canadian seedgrowers found out what its proposed charges will be; and the small meat processors found out what its proposed charges will be, but there is no method for them to consult to discover whether they are all being charged 10 or 15 times more, or whether some are being charged only three or four times more.
The Department ensured that the information that went out was very limited. As a result, I contend that proper consultation cannot take place. I contend that it is the intention of the Government to charge this tax. There is no consultation on that. The parameters in which the consultation takes place are very limited. Therefore, real consultation cannot take place, so it is simply a sham.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Employment and Immigration
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, as the Hon. Member pointed out earlier, the new inspection services fee schedule is not yet in itself a proposition; one should look
Adjournment Debate
up in the dictionary the meaning of a proposition which is the object of consultation, and one ought to be careful when talking about a firm intention. The whole matter is now under consideration by the people concerned.
We made a proposition and the industry took it under advisement. We are now discussing every detail of this matter with the groups involved, and we know there might be some difficulties. That is why we meet with the major national associations to seek their views and suggestions. We have said many times, and I say again, that we are consulting the industry before implementing new charges.
The Hon. Member is asking me why we are undertaking this cost-recovery program. It is quite simple, Mr. Speaker, and the answer is obvious-the deficit has to come down. From our discussions with the industry, we know that the agricultural community shares this concern and is anxious to cooperate to reduce the national debt, and that protects them, as it does the consumer and the agricultural production industry. They agree they have their share of responsibilities.
We are therefore convinced that together we can find an acceptable solution which will help us lower the deficit while at the same time cushioning its impact on Canadian producers. If we refer to the November 8 economic statement, it is true that some measures have been adopted, but the Government is now in a consultation process concerning various measures with a view to adapting the general principle to each specific case.

subtopic: UNEMPLOYMENT INSURANCE-PETITION AGAINST CALCULATION OF SEVERANCE PAY. (B) DISCUSSION PAPER INQUIRY
UNEMPLOYMENT INSURANCE-PETITION AGAINST CALCULATION OF SEVERANCE PAY. (B) DISCUSSION PAPER INQUIRY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I would like to follow up on a question I asked the Minister of Employment and Immigration (Miss MacDonald) on March 25 concerning changes to the Unemployment Insurance Act.
The November 8 economic statement included an announcement that severance pay and accumulated pension income would be considered as earnings when people apply for unemployment insurance benefits. This would have the effect of delaying, for many weeks, the time when a person could begin to draw unemployment insurance. At that time the Government reckoned that these changes would save it $90 million.
I have great difficulty with this, Mr. Speaker. While I recognize the Government's concern about the deficit and its desire to move on that in a responsible fashion, I cannot see these particular measures as responsible in our particular situation of high unemployment. Until now a person could receive income amounting to up to 25 per cent of their UI benefits. It may seem logical, to a point, that people be required to use severance pay to deal with their expenses until they relocate. However, in times of high unemployment one would question the wisdom of requiring people to use up their severance pay before claiming for unemployment insurance.
3600

April 1, 1985
Adjournment Debate
In these times of high unemployment, people must be mobile and resourceful. Given a little freedom to use their severance pay, some people would probably relocate to an area where they may have a better chance of finding employment. They might use it in some other way to help become re-employed, such as by investing in tools or other work related equipment.
Under the present situation, when people become unemployed and know they will be unemployed for some time, the Government is essentially forcing them to use all of their severance pay to deal with the necessities of life, and thereby perhaps inadvertently interfere with their opportunity to become re-employed.
There were many complaints after the economic statement of November 8 and the Minister has made some adjustments. For instance, there will be exceptions in cases where severance pay is part of a collective agreement or written employee-employer's policy within certain dates. The question of using returned pension contributions has been postponed to January 1. However, this is a matter about which I feel most strongly, a matter which I hope the Minister will not only postpone but will eliminate completely.
According to the new policy, a person who is under 45 years of age and loses his or her job will have pension contributions returned. Obviously, pension contributions for people over 45 are locked in, or vested. If a person receives $3,000 back from a pension fund and his or her normal earnings were $300 a week, that person is now deemed to have ten weeks income. Therefore, the claim for unemployment insurance is postponed for ten weeks.
Surely this is very unwise because we expect people to save for their future. When most people become unemployed they do all they can to make the severance pay and unemployment insurance cover current expenses until they get rehired. They try to keep the returned pension contributions for investment either in a new employer plan or an RRSP in order to provide for their future.
When this plan was originally announced by the Government on November 8, there were many vigorous complaints; complaints from unions, and complaints from companies in the process of negotiating early retirement packages for their employees. They saw their plans thrown into turmoil because these changes amount to a disincentive to early retirement.
The Minister has agreed to postpone to January 1 the Implementation of the requirement that people use up their interim pension contributions. I am sure that the Minister,
who is a compassionate woman, does not have her heart in this requirement. I am sure it is the hawks in her Cabinet who are forcing this measure on her. I sincerely hope some way will be found to drop this measure.
We all know that Canada is a nation of savers. It is difficult to get by if one is over 65 and must rely on government assistance. It is unacceptable for the government to expect people who are out of work to mortgage their futures, to use for the necessities of life that money they are contributing to a pension fund for their retirement. How many will be deprived of a dignified retirement by this ill-considered measure if it is enforced? I sincerely hope that after January 1 wisdom will prevail and we will see the end of it.
